Done at Brussels, For the Commission The President EN 17 EN 4 Accompanying documents 4.1 Impact Assessment with cost-benefit analysis Introduction As per Article 49(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1620, before submitting draft RTS to the Commission, AMLA shall conduct open public consultations and analyse the potential related costs and benefits. This analysis presents the Impact Assessment with Cost-Benefit Analysis (IA/CBA) of the main policy options included in the final report on the draft RTS under Article 46(4) of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 on the respective duties of the home and host supervisors, and the modalities of cooperation between them within the anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) supervisory system for the purposes of group supervision.

This IA/CBA is qualitative in nature and the policy choices have been taken in accordance with qualitative considerations, based on input obtained from the financial supervisors and the non- financial supervisors to which the draft RTS is addressed. A. Problem identification The previous AML/CFT framework relied on the transposition, by Member States, of high-level AML/CFT standards set out in Directive (EU) 2015/849. This proved insufficient to tackle the inherently cross-border nature of financial crime, which can be effectively addressed only through an integrated and harmonised approach at Union level, along with strong cooperation between supervisors across jurisdictions.

Directive (EU) 2015/849 included a general requirement for supervisors of home and host Member States to cooperate, which was subsequently strengthened. Moreover, although the European Supervisory Authorities issued guidelines on AML/CFT colleges in 20196, these guidelines do not cover all types of home-host relationships in the context of group AML/CFT supervision. In practice, significant divergences in supervisory practices exist across Member States, alongside the absence of sufficiently robust arrangements for cross-border cooperation and information exchange between supervisors, creating persistent challenges for group-level supervision, especially in those situations where an AML/CFT college is not established.

In such cases, cooperation has often been relying on bilateral and ad hoc agreements, resulting in significant operational burden for supervisors and creating frictions to information flows. Cooperation challenges may also be present in the non-financial sector, due to the marked 6 Joint Guidelines on cooperation and information exchange for the purpose of Directive (EU) 2015/849 between competent authorities supervising credit and financial institutions. EN 18 EN heterogeneity of its sub-sectors and the divergent approaches to supervisory set-ups in parts of it. Cooperation between supervisors is essential to ensure a common supervisory approach across the Union and represents a prerequisite for the effective functioning of the AML/CFT supervisory system.

It is therefore necessary to establish a robust and harmonised framework governing cooperation between supervisors, including provisions to ensure timely and secure information exchange. This will notably enhance the effectiveness of supervision of obliged entities that form part of cross-border groups. Under Directive (EU) 2024/1640, supervisors of the home Member State and those of the host Member State should cooperate to the greatest extent possible and regardless of their respective nature or status.

Furthermore, the Directive mandates the establishment of AML/CFT supervisory colleges in the financial sector with respect to obliged entities that operate in several Member States through establishments and with respect to obliged entities which are part of a cross- border group, and encourages such colleges in the non-financial sector. However, it remains necessary to clarify the precise responsibilities of home and host supervisors and provide a harmonised cooperation framework, especially in group-supervision scenarios where no AML/CFT college is set up.

To this end, Article 46(4) of Directive 2024/1640 requires AMLA, in light of its coordinating role, to develop a draft RTS detailing the respective duties of home and host supervisors of groups and the modalities of cooperation between them, in the absence of detailed provisions in the Directive and other regulatory instruments. B. Policy objectives These draft RTS aims to support the effective functioning of the AML/CFT supervisory system, by establishing a framework for cooperation and information exchange between supervisors of the home Member State and supervisors of the host Member State in contexts of group supervision, in the financial and non-financial sectors.

The draft RTS applies to the supervision of groups, without prejudice to more specific or different provisions to be applied where AML/CFT colleges are established in accordance with Articles 49 and 50 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640. More specifically, the draft RTS establishes the framework to ensure effective cooperation in group-level supervision scenarios between home and host supervisors. It defines their respective duties and responsibilities along with cooperation modalities. It details practical arrangements with regards to the conduct of inquiries, carrying out activities in accordance with agreed coordinated approaches and exchanging information, where such information is not covered by legal privilege.

The draft RTS fosters timely and relevant cooperation between home and host supervisors, while safeguarding confidentiality and data protection obligations. C. Baseline scenario EN 19 EN The baseline scenario would foresee the application of a number of provisions on the cooperation between home and host supervisors for the purposes of AML/CFT supervision of groups, as specified in Article 46 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640. In particular, Article 46(1) requires Member States to ensure that supervisors of the home Member State and those of the host Member State cooperate with each other to the greatest extent possible, and cooperate with AMLA when acting as a supervisor.

Furthermore, under Article 46(2), Member States must ensure that home supervisors supervise the effective implementation of the group-wide policies, procedures and controls, while host Member State supervisors supervise the compliance of the establishments located in their territory. Moreover, Article 46(3) requires Member States to ensure that supervisors provide one another with any information necessary for the exercise of their supervisory tasks – whether on request or on their own initiative – and especially any information necessary for the assessment of the inherent or residual risk exposure of an obliged entity in another Member State.

Lastly, Member States shall ensure that the same provisions apply to the groups of obliged entities in the financial and non-financial sectors, according to Article 46(6). Article 46 of the Directive (EU) 2024/1640 does not provide any further details about the respective responsibilities of home and host supervisors or the modalities of cooperation between them. This gap might create legal and operational uncertainties that could weaken the efficiency and effectiveness of cooperation between supervisors of the home Member State supervisors and the supervisors of the host Member State in context of group supervision.

In particular, the absence of clear and harmonised provisions on cooperation modalities would increase operational burden on supervisors, who would need to rely on bilateral and ad hoc cooperation agreements. Another risk is that information may simply fail to reach the requesting supervisor where the requested one does not respond, creating de facto gaps in supervisory coverage that no existing provision addresses. This would also undermine cooperation and in particular information sharing, which could, in turn, erode the robustness and efficacy of supervision of groups with cross-border operations. D.

Options considered, cost-benefit analysis, and preferred option This section describes the main policy options considered and the decisions taken by AMLA as part of the development of the draft RTS on cooperation between home and host supervisors for the purposes of cross-border group supervision. This section starts by outlining the overarching approach guiding the policy decisions. Then, it presents the main policy options considered for each policy issue addressed by the draft RTS, followed by an analysis of the potential costs and benefits of each option from a qualitative perspective, concluding with the preferred options resulting from the analysis.

Overarching principles As overall approach when drafting the policy mandate, AMLA has sought to strike an appropriate balance between granular and flexible provisions. More specifically, the draft RTS sets out EN 20 EN provisions applying to the supervision of groups of obliged entities in the financial and non- financial sector operating across borders, including practical arrangements for supervisory cooperation, particularly in the context of information exchange, inquiries and coordinated supervisory approaches. These provisions aim to ensure legal and operational clarity, reducing the need for supervisors to negotiate bilateral agreements for cooperation and information exchange, while supporting a more harmonised Union-wide approach.

At the same time, the draft RTS allows for an appropriate degree of flexibility, thereby limiting unnecessary regulatory burden for supervisors and enhancing administrative efficiency. The draft RTS also aims to ensure continuity and coherence with existing EU regulatory instruments regarding supervisory cooperation and information exchange where this is warranted, such as the EBA's Guidelines on AML/CFT Colleges7 and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/17228. Policy issue 1: Horizontal or sectoral approach The provisions related to cooperation in the context of group supervision set out in Article 46 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 apply to the financial and non-financial sectors. Accordingly, the draft RTS under Article 46(4) is intended to apply across both sectors as well.

AMLA therefore assessed whether the draft RTS should be fully horizontal or complemented with sector-specific provisions. Two options were considered: A. Adopting a horizontal approach; B. Adopting a horizontal approach, with sector-specific provisions where needed. Under Option A, the draft RTS would contain a single set of provisions applying equally to financial and non-financial supervisors. This option would entail several benefits. It would ensure the maximum harmonisation of cooperation modalities between supervisors in the financial and non-financial sector, reducing fragmentation and fostering convergence and consistency in supervisory practices.

This would provide benefits in terms of effectiveness of cooperation, and ensure adherence to the harmonisation objective pursued by the new EU AML/CFT framework. This approach would also promote a simplification of the legal framework, by providing a single set of risk-based, proportionate and principle-based provisions, thereby facilitating implementation and reducing interpretative divergence. 7 Joint guidelines on cooperation and information exchange for the purpose of Directive (EU) 2015/849 between competent authorities supervising credit and financial institutions (The AML/CFT Colleges).

8 Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/1722 of 18 June 2021 supplementing Directive (EU) 2015/2366 of the European Parliament and of the Council with regard to regulatory technical standards specifying the framework for cooperation and the exchange of information between competent authorities of the home and the host Member States in the context of supervision of payment institutions and electronic money institutions exercising cross-border provision of payment services. EN 21 EN The only limitation linked to this approach is that it would imply keeping the provisions high-level enough to encompass a wide range of cross-border situations.

Under Option B, the draft RTS would retain a common core of harmonised provisions applicable to both the financial and non-financial sector, while introducing targeted sector-specific provisions to address identified differences in supervisory structures or arrangements. In terms of benefits, this approach would ensure harmonisation to the maximum extent possible, while addressing sectoral specificities through targeted provisions, where deemed necessary and duly justified. This could improve operational fit in selected contexts where supervisory structures or arrangements materially differ. However, this approach would introduce additional layers of complexity and could create inconsistencies across sectors.

In addition, the introduction of separate provisions for different sectors could complicate cooperation between supervisors in the contexts cross-sectoral group structures and reduce the benefits of a single, coherent cooperation framework. Given the considerations explained above, Option A was chosen. The draft RTS adopts a fully horizontal approach, establishing a single coherent framework to support timely and effective cooperation between supervisors in the context of cross-border groups of obliged entities in the financial and non-financial sector. This approach supports supervisory convergence through harmonised supervisory practices, in line with the objectives of the AML/CFT framework, while also promoting simplification of the legal framework.

To ensure proportionality across the full range of supervisory contexts, the draft RTS specifies that the provisions should be applied having regard to the size, risk profile and operational characteristics of the supervised group, as well as to the capacities of the cooperating supervisors. Policy issue 2: Scope of cooperation Article 46(4) of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 requires the draft RTS to specify the respective duties of the home and host supervisors, and the modalities of cooperation between them. When defining the scope of cooperation, AMLA considered the following options: A. General cooperation framework, including only general, principle-based provisions; B. General cooperation framework, with specific provisions on the main types of cooperation.

Under Option A, the draft RTS would establish a broad cooperation framework consisting of principle-based provisions, without distinguishing between different types of cooperation. In terms of benefits, this approach would provide a high level of flexibility for supervisors, which would retain discretion to select and calibrate cooperation modalities, and adopt targeted practical arrangements, on a case-by-case basis, facilitating context-specific solutions. EN 22 EN However, this approach would not provide sufficient legal certainty and operational clarity for supervisors regarding the modalities of cooperation between them. In the absence of clear expectations, supervisors may adopt divergent approaches, which could potentially hinder timely and effective cross-border cooperation.

Moreover, where the framework is too high-level, supervisors may still need to negotiate bilateral arrangements to agree practical cooperation modalities. This would reduce administrative efficiency and create operational and administrative costs for supervisors. Under Option B, the draft RTS would contain general provisions applicable to all situations in the context of group supervision, complemented by targeted provisions for the most relevant and recurrent types of cooperation. This option would entail significant benefits. A common framework would ensure effective cooperation through the entire supervisory cycle, enhance harmonisation, and promote convergence and consistency of cooperation practices.

At the same time, specific provisions would provide additional guidance regarding the most recurrent and relevant forms of cooperation, thus enhancing legal clarity and increasing operational efficiency. However, this option implies a modest increase in complexity. This cost is considered negligible, since the reduced flexibility for supervisors would be offset by the greater legal clarity and operational efficiency provided by this approach. Given the assessment outlined above, Option B was adopted. The draft RTS provides common provisions applicable to all situations in the context of group supervision, complemented by targeted provisions on the most relevant and recurrent cooperation modalities, namely information exchange, coordinated supervisory approaches, and inquiries.

The draft RTS also specifies that information covered by legal privilege falls outside the scope of this cooperation framework, as it does not relate to the exercise of supervisory activities. Overall, this approach provides a streamlined, proportionate, and harmonised framework ensuring effective cooperation in the context of group supervision, while ensuring legal clarity and operational efficiency. Policy issue 3: Consent and permissible use of information Effective AML/CFT supervision of groups of obliged entities requires timely information exchange among supervisors, while ensuring compliance with professional secrecy and confidentiality requirements when information is disclosed.

When addressing consent and permissible use of information, AMLA considered the following policy options: A. Restricting information disclosure, requiring prior consent for all situations in which information is disclosed; B. Facilitating information disclosure, requiring notification rather than prior consent for information disclosure within the EU supervisory system, except in those cases where the information originates from a third-country counterpart. EN 23 EN Under Option A, the draft RTS would require prior consent from the supervisor which originated the information in all cases in which information is disclosed. The main benefit of this approach is that it does not imply any changes with respect to the current regulatory framework, thus avoiding any adaptation costs.

However, requiring consent for all types of disclosure of information would impose excessive burden on supervisors, resulting in disproportionate administrative costs and potentially impairing timely information flows. The administrative friction might reduce the scope and speed of information disclosure, ultimately undermining the effectiveness of cooperation in the context of group supervision. Under Option B, the draft RTS would not require prior consent to disclose information to other EU supervisors, AMLA acting as supervisor, and public authorities overseeing SRBs, except in those cases where the information originated from a third-country counterpart. However, a notification requirement would be introduced.

The same would apply to cases where onward disclosure is authorised or required under Union law. In terms of benefits, this option would reduce administrative costs associated with information- sharing and facilitate timely information exchanges in the context of group supervision, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of cooperation. At the same time, limiting the scope of application of this provision to the EU supervisory context, along with introducing a notification requirement, would preserve trust among supervisors. Although this option would reduce the level of ex ante control by the originating authority for intra- EU onward disclosures, this would be counterbalanced by the need to facilitate information flows and enhance cooperation within the EU.

Given the considerations outlined above, Option B was chosen. This option facilitates information disclosure in the context of group supervision, thus increasing the effectiveness of cooperation, while still preserving trust among supervisors and ensuring data protection and compliance with professional secrecy and confidentiality requirements. 4.2 Feedback on the public consultation AMLA held a public hearing on 28 May 2026 to consult on the draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) specifying the respective duties of home and host supervisors and the modalities of cooperation between them, as mandated by Article 46(4) of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 (AMLD).

Approximately 150 participants attended the hearing, representing financial institutions, non- financial sector operators, industry associations, and practitioners active across multiple Member States and jurisdictions. EN 24 EN 4.2.1 SUMMARY OF KEY ISSUES AND AMLA’S RESPONSE The sections below set out requests and comments by themes, and AMLA’s response. Where relevant, they also describe how the draft RTS has been, or may be, amended or supplemented to address the points raised. Multi-jurisdictional operations and supervisory convergence Concerns were raised about how to navigate situations where different national supervisors hold conflicting interpretations of AML/CFT obligations or diverge in the application of exemptions.

For an institution operating in several jurisdictions simultaneously, the absence of a harmonised baseline creates compliance uncertainty and operational complexity. AMLA’s response Beyond the RTS itself, which focuses on home-host cooperation, AMLA is developing a supervisory methodology in cooperation with Member States, designed to further align supervisory approaches and reduce divergence in interpretation. More broadly, supervisory cooperation can support supervisory efficiency and convergence of practices across the Single Market.

Groups with offshore or non-financial entities A question was raised on how the cooperation framework would apply to groups that include an EU-regulated financial institution alongside a subsidiary in an offshore jurisdiction and non- financial entities, i.e., mixed structures that straddle the EU supervisory perimeter. AMLA’s response The RTS applies to supervisors of obliged entities in both the financial and non-financial sectors that form part of a cross-border group, and will be part of a broader supervisory cooperation framework. For larger groups, AML/CFT supervisory colleges may be established, with specific provisions governing cooperation in that context.

In addition, AMLA is working on Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with supervisors in non-EU jurisdictions and with prudential supervisors. Information Exchange Protocols Interrogations were raised about the protocols governing information requests and responses between supervisors, notably how the current framework would evolve in the 2027 landscape, and whether a common framework could make follow-up exchanges more effective. AMLA’s response The draft RTS sets out concrete modalities for information exchange. AMLA is also thinking about tools to support a more integrated common framework. The overarching aim is to provide a simple and efficient framework for supervisory cooperation.

EN 25 EN Group definition and scope Questions were raised about the applicable definition of “group” for the purposes of the RTS, specifically whether it refers to the AMLR definition or that in the RTS on group-wide policies, and structures that have to apply group-wide requirements (entities sharing common ownership, management or compliance control, including networks or partnerships) fall within the scope of the instrument. AMLA’s response Article 46 AMLD encourages supervisors responsible for obliged entities in group-like structures to cooperate and exchange information, but does not formally bring those structures within the mandatory scope of the RTS.

Group-like structures may apply the provisions of the RTS on a voluntary basis, as those procedures represent a structured and operationally sound framework for supervisory cooperation. AMLA noted that these structures are nonetheless included in the AML/CFT college framework foreseen under the AMLD.

Risks of conflicting guidance, lead supervisor identification, and language barriers Issues were raised on (i) whether guidance on group-like structures in the non-financial sector would be addressed in the RTS or in separate instruments, (ii) what hierarchy applies when a home supervisor and multiple host supervisors issue conflicting guidance, and whether a clear lead supervisor designation would provide legal certainty for obliged entities, and (iii) on language barriers and the related operational difficulties. AMLA’s response Within the AML/CFT college framework, a lead supervisor will be designated, providing a structured mechanism for coordinating supervisory approaches.

As regards group-like structures, the RTS under Article 46(4) AMLD is not binding for them, but they may apply its provisions on a voluntary basis, while they are included within the college framework foreseen under the AMLD. On language, although the RTS does not prescribe the language of supervisory communications, agreeing on practicable modalities of cooperation, including language, and find ways to understand each other, it will be part of enhancing a form of cooperation culture among supervisors.

Proportionality and avoidance of duplicative reporting Concerns were raised about smaller obliged entities potentially facing duplicative reporting obligations when subject to information requests from multiple supervisors across jurisdictions, and about the importance of ensuring proportionality. AMLA’s response Proportionality is a core principle embedded in the draft RTS and will continue to inform the drafting of other instruments forming part of the broader supervisory cooperation framework, EN 26 EN including those governing AML/CFT colleges. In operational terms, the RTS reflects this principle by for instance requiring supervisors to verify whether requested information is already accessible before submitting requests to their counterparts.

This approach is designed to keep cooperation requests targeted and proportionate. More broadly, the aim is to provide a simple and efficient framework for supervisory cooperation that, by promoting better coordination among supervisors, can also contribute to limiting the burden of duplicative requests on obliged entities.

37 F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 2 1 Executive Summary In order to strengthen the Union’s framework for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT), Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) aims to harmonise the preventative measures to be put in place at Union level.

Articles 16 and 17 AMLR cover the regulatory obligations regarding the design and implementation of group-wide AML/CFT frameworks, including their application across cross-border group structures and in situations where branches or subsidiaries operate in third countries. The purpose of the mandates under Articles 16(4) and 17(3) AMLR is to clarify further these obligations in draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS). The draft RTS contain requirements that specify further the framework and content of group-wide requirements. In addition to minimum general requirement, the draft RTS define provisions related to information sharing among entities of a group.

Furthermore, they provide criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in cases of two or more obliged entities in the Union belonging to a head office in a third country and they are not in a parent/subsidiary relationship. They also provide conditions to apply group-wide requirements to structures other than groups and criteria to identify the head of the structure in these cases. This extension represents a significant development, particularly for the non- financial sector where such arrangements are common. The draft RTS ensure a proportionate and risk- based approach, ensuring applicability across both financial and non-financial sector groups.

The mandates under Articles 16(4) and 17(3) AMLR are inherently interlinked, reinforcing each other through cross-reference obligations and complementary requirements. AMLA therefore proposes to draft a single set of draft RTS to address both mandates in a cohesive and simplified manner. Such a single instrument ensures regulatory coherence, avoids duplication between related provisions and provides obliged entities with a clearer and more consistent framework for implementing group-wide AML/CFT requirements across the Union. In preparing this final report, AMLA sought and considered input from national supervisors across both financial and non-financial sectors and engaged with private sector representatives.

AMLA further enhanced the final report by considering the responses provided by respondents collected through the public consultation conducted between 16 April and 15 June 2026. These draft RTS are part of a broader set of AMLA instruments that will be delivered and that will touch upon the AML/CFT requirements of obliged entities. AMLA will continue its endeavors to place proportionality and the risk-based approach at the heart of this work and ensure the effectiveness of the instruments to be delivered while simplifying AML/CFT compliance for obliged entities where possible. 1.1 Next steps The draft RTS will be submitted to the European Commission for adoption before being published in the Official Journal of the European Union.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 3 2 Background and rationale 2.1 General provisions Article 16 AMLR establishes the core obligations for group-wide AML/CFT frameworks, requiring parent undertakings to implement uniform policies, controls and procedures across all entities under their responsibility. It also mandates the establishment of a group compliance function and the adoption of an annual report on the implementation of these group-wide policies. Finally, it requires effective sharing of information within entities of a group.

Article 16(4) AMLR requires AMLA to develop draft RTS specifying: ▪ the minimum requirements of group-wide policies, procedures and controls, including minimum standards for information sharing within the group; ▪ the criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the cases covered by Article 2(1), point (42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. ▪ the conditions under which the provisions of Article 16 AMLR apply to entities that are part of structures which share common ownership, management or compliance control, including networks or partnerships, as well as the criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in those cases.

Article 17 AMLR complements the group-wide framework established under Article 16 AMLR by addressing situations where branches or subsidiaries located in third countries cannot fully implement group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls due to restrictions in local laws applicable in a third country. Article 17 AMLR requires parent undertakings or obliged entities to implement additional measures where legal or regulatory restrictions in a third country prevent compliance with the AMLR and to inform the supervisor of the home Member State of such impediments.

Where those measures are insufficient to effectively manage the risk of ML/TF, supervisors of the home Member State may require the implementation of further supervisory actions, including restrictions on business relationships, the termination of transactions, or the closure of operations in the relevant third country. Article 17(3) AMLR therefore mandates AMLA to develop RTS specifying: ▪ the type of additional measures to be taken by obliged entities where the law of a third country prevents compliance with the AMLR, ▪ the minimum actions that must be implemented in such circumstances, and ▪ the additional supervisory actions that may be applied by supervisors where the measures taken are insufficient.

The provisions in the draft RTS fulfil the mandates in Articles 16 and 17 AMLR and establish high-level balanced group-wide requirements, which are compatible with existing (financial sector) requirements and guidelines. 2.2 AMLA’s approach - focus on simplification F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 4 In developing these RTS and taking into account the feedback received during the public consultation, AMLA sought to establish a simplified, proportionate and risk-based framework under the AMLR whenever possible.

In particular, AMLA aimed to reduce unnecessary complexity, regulatory burden and compliance costs by establishing a single horizontal framework applicable across obliged entities in both the financial and non-financial sectors.

To achieve this objective, AMLA: ▪ refrains from sector-specifying requirements where the AMLR already provides sufficient detail; ▪ maintains flexibility by setting out measures and options that obliged entities may consider when determining the most effective and proportionate approach to compliance; ▪ streamlines closely related requirements falling within AMLA's regulatory mandate; ▪ seeks to ensure consistency with existing supervisory expectations and established standards while reflecting AMLA's mandate under the AMLR and the feedback received from stakeholders ▪ establishes a transitory regime for the first application of notifications set in Sections 5 and 6 to supervisors.

In preparing these draft RTS, AMLA assessed the relevant provisions of the AMLR, the EBA's advice to the European Commission, as well as inputs received from public and private sector stakeholders. This assessment was undertaken to identify areas where further clarification, simplification or refinement was necessary to support the effective and consistent application of the AMLR. AMLA also engaged with national competent authorities from the financial and non-financial sectors, the European Commission, EBA and representatives of obliged entities. AMLA furthermore considered the feedback received through the public consultation conducted between 16 April and 15 June 2026 and refined the draft RTS where appropriate in light of the responses received.

Definitions (Section 1) The draft RTS introduce a definition of the term ‘structure’ for the purposes of ensuring a consistent interpretation and application of the requirements set out in the draft RTS. Following the public consultation and AMLA’s further assessment of the draft RTS, several definitions included in the Consultation Paper have been removed. AMLA considered that these definitions were not necessary to achieve the objectives of the draft RTS, taking into account stakeholders’ feedback and the need to avoid unnecessary regulatory complexity. Minimum requirements regarding group-wide policies, procedures and controls (Section 2) The draft RTS further specify the group-wide requirements referred to in Article 16 AMLR.

Article 16 AMLR requires parent undertakings in the Union to ensure that policies, procedures and controls are implemented consistently across all branches and subsidiaries within the group. The draft RTS provide rules setting out a clear governance framework, including the allocation of responsibilities, reporting lines and arrangements between relevant functions to ensure that relevant information is shared effectively across the group. To support the effective implementation of these obligations, the draft RTS also clarify that group-wide policies and procedures should be appropriately documented, kept up to date and made available to supervisors upon request.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 5 In light of the feedback received during the public consultation, AMLA streamlined and simplified this section of the draft RTS, while retaining the elements necessary to ensure the consistent and effective application of group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls. Information sharing within a group (Section 3) Effective information sharing is a cornerstone of the draft RTS, reflecting the principles outlined by the EBA as part of its response to the Commission’s call for advice issued in October 2025.

The draft RTS set a broad list of information that when relevant under the AML/CFT framework may be shared within groups, enabling obliged entities to detect and mitigate cross-border ML/TF risks more effectively. The draft RTS nonetheless make clear that such sharing must be conducted in line with certain standards such as on a “need to know” basis, with appropriate safeguards to ensure compliance with data protection regulation and ensuring confidentiality and security. Additional provisions clarify the approach to the sharing of information to and from third countries when information sharing takes place from the perspective of obliged entities of the group in the Union.

Following the public consultation, AMLA revised this section and moved the specific pieces of information to Annex I setting out the categories and types of information to be shared within a group. AMLA also amended the drafting of Section 3 to improve clarity and further reflect the principles of simplification and proportionality in the text, also in view of stakeholders’ comments. Legal impediments affecting branches and subsidiaries in third countries (Section 4) Groups subject to the AMLR frequently operate through branches or subsidiaries established in third countries. In some jurisdictions, local legal or regulatory frameworks may restrict the ability of OEs to implement group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls.

Such impediments may arise, for example, from national data protection rules, banking secrecy provisions, restrictions on the sharing of suspicious transaction information, or limitations on access to customer or beneficial ownership information. Article 17 AMLR establishes a harmonised Union-level framework for managing such situations. Where the law of a third country does not permit compliance with the AMLR, parent undertakings or obliged entities are required to implement minimum actions, including additional measures, to ensure that branches and subsidiaries effectively manage ML/TF risks.

The draft RTS build on the framework established by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/758, while extending its scope to all obliged entities under the AMLR, including the non-financial sectors. This approach ensures continuity with the existing regulatory framework while updating it to reflect the broader scope and supervisory architecture introduced by the AMLR. However, the previous structure has been simplified and the mention to specific legal impediments has been removed along with the prescriptive additional measures for each one of those scenarios.

The draft RTS introduce provisions on additional supervisory actions and establish a structured escalation framework to be applied where supervisors determine, following a supervisory assessment, that the measures taken are insufficient to effectively manage the risk. Where risks arising from third- country impediments are considered remediable, supervisors may require corrective measures, including the submission and implementation of risk-mitigation plans, and monitor their F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 6 implementation.

Where risks are deemed unmanageable, the framework provides for stronger supervisory interventions, including restrictions on business relationships or occasional transactions, and ultimately the closure of some or all operations in the affected jurisdiction. Following the public consultation, AMLA simplified and streamlined Section 4 by reducing the number of articles from seven to three and removing the mention to specific legal impediments with rigid requirements. The revised structure aligns the provisions more closely with the AMLR mandate, with separate articles addressing minimum actions, additional measures and supervisory actions. This approach improves clarity, reduces complexity and further reflects the principles of simplification and proportionality underpinning the draft RTS.

Criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in cases of two or more obliged entities whose head office is located outside of the Union (Section 5) The draft RTS introduce criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in cases where two or more obliged entities established in the Union have a common head office located outside of the Union and where there is no parent-subsidiary relationship among the obliged entities (sister or affiliate entities). The draft RTS provide a clear methodology for determining which obliged entity should be identified as parent undertaking and assume responsibility for group-wide requirements.

The quantitative and qualitative criteria set in the draft RTS focus on decision-making powers, controls and risk management capacity, ensuring that the identified obliged entity is the best positioned obliged entity to enforce AML/CFT measures across the group as a parent undertaking. This also ensures that the identified obliged entity has the necessary resources and influence to implement and monitor compliance effectively. To prevent regulatory uncertainty, the draft RTS introduce a notification obligation and supervisory assessment, requiring the obliged entity identified as the parent undertaking to notify its role to the relevant supervisor. This mechanism ensures transparency and allows supervisors to identify and address potential gaps in compliance oversight.

In light of the feedback received during the public consultation, AMLA streamlined and simplified this section of the draft RTS, while retaining the elements necessary to ensure the consistent and effective identification of the parent undertaking in the Union in the cases where there is no parent-subsidiary relationship among the obliged entities in the Union belonging to the same head office in a third country.

Conditions for the application of group-wide requirements to structure sharing common ownership, management or compliance controls (Section 6) The draft RTS clarify the extension of the scope of group-wide requirements from traditionally defined groups under accounting or prudential regimes to structures that, while not formally organised as groups, exhibit characteristics that warrant similar AML/CFT requirements. This includes networks, partnerships, or franchises where the structure has two or more obliged entities that operate under common ownership, management, or compliance controls or a combination of them.

The recitals, definitions, and criteria set out in the draft RTS are specifically designed to provide obliged entities, particularly those in the non-financial sector, with clear, actionable guidance to determine F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 7 whether they fall within the scope of these provisions. The objective is to effectively target structures where the application of group-wide AML/CFT measures is both necessary and proportionate. In addition to defining the scope of application, the draft RTS also provide criteria for identifying the head of the structure for these structures. The criteria are built mainly to recognise the powers and controls of one entity in the structure.

To maintain regulatory clarity, the draft RTS introduce a notification requirement to the supervisors and supervisory assessment. This mechanism ensures that supervisors are aware of the identified entity acting as head of the structure and can monitor compliance of group-wide requirements effectively in such structures. First notification to supervisors shall take place no later than six months after the application of the RTS. Under justified circumstances and to recognise proportionality, the draft RTS address situations in structures where obliged entities identify a non-obliged entity as the head or where there are legal impediments for the identification of the head.

The draft RTS introduce a supervisory mechanism that allows obliged entities not to identify the head of the structure under certain conditions to ensure that certain minimum group-wide requirements still apply to them. In case the permission is granted, the application of group-wide requirements would be limited to certain minimum group-wide requirements that obliged entities would mutually comply with without requiring group-wide steering of one designated obliged entity acting as head of the structure. First notification to supervisors shall take place no later than six months after the application of the RTS.

In light of the feedback received during the public consultation, AMLA clarified the provisions in this section of the draft RTS, while retaining the elements necessary to ensure the consistent and effective application of group-wide requirements to structures other than groups having common ownership, management, compliance control or a combination of them. In addition, AMLA recognized proportionality in the application of group-wide requirements to structure other than groups in the absence of a head of the structure being an obliged entity, while still ensuring minimum application of certain group-wide requirements in this situation.

Articles 16(4) and 17(3) thereof, Whereas: (1) Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 aims for the harmonisation of the measures to be put in place to prevent money laundering, its predicate offences, terrorist financing and the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions at the Union level, including when such measures are designed and implemented in groups or in structures other than groups when such structures fulfil the conditions set out in this Regulation.

Minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls should be developed, implemented and applied at the group level in an adequate and consistent manner, while avoiding any risks of compromising anti-money laundering, counterterrorism financing as well as preventing the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions.

(2) Group-wide policies, procedures and controls should be designed to ensure consistency in the implementation of the group-wide requirements mentioned in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, for example by enhancing governance arrangements; the standing and role of the compliance manager and, where applicable, those of the compliance officer at the level of the group; the relations between the parent undertaking and the subsidiaries and branches in the Union and in third countries; and the development and implementation of group-wide risk assessments. (3) At the same time, group-wide policies, procedures and controls should not result in a derogation for the parent undertaking in the Union from implementing the entity-level policies, procedures and controls, including its entity-level risk assessment. In any case, information sharing should take into account the requirements set out in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on information accompanying transfers of funds and certain crypto-assets and amending Directive (EU) 2015/8492 and any administrative act of the supervisors. (6) Obliged entities should use the information shared by other entities in the group to make, among other things, informed decisions on customers, transactions and risk assessments, and to potentially restrict or refuse to enter into a new relationship, terminate existing business relationships or restrict or refuse to carry out the execution of occasional transactions in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

Furthermore, the information shared within the group should be used to prevent and mitigate money laundering, terrorist financing and the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions and to inform the parent undertaking in the Union of the group-wide-level risk assessment. (7) Information sharing should also include ad hoc sharing of newly identified relevant information related to the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions. (8) The Union anti-money-laundering / countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) framework applies to a wide variety of obliged entities.

Some obliged entities perform transactions; other obliged entities, such as real estate agents, lawyers and notaries, provide services or activities connected to transactions. For these obliged entities, information- sharing requirements should include sharing of information related to the provision of services or activities under the AML/CFT framework. (9) Certain aspects of the implementation of the AML/CFT framework involve the collection, analysis, storage and sharing of data, including personal data. The processing of personal data should be permitted only for the purposes of the prevention and management of money laundering, terrorist financing and the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions.

In addition, information sharing should be subject to sufficient guarantees in terms of confidentiality, secure channels and data protection in line with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation)3 regarding the use of information and should fully respect fundamental rights. (10) Sharing of information should be implemented in a manner proportionate to the relevancy of the request and be based on a need-to-know assessment.

In any case, obliged entities should not be prevented from sharing any relevant information related to risks of money 2 OJ L 150, 9.6.2023, p. 1. 3 OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1. (11) Obliged entities in the Union may share information with other entities of the group outside the Union.

In such cases, the Regulation clarifies that in cases where there are restrictions or prohibitions on the sharing of information to third countries, the parent undertaking in the Union and the other obliged entities of the group in the Union need to assess the restrictions and prohibitions and communicate them to the supervisors in the Union. In any case, obliged entities should take appropriate measures to address such restrictions or prohibitions on sharing information.

(12) There are circumstances where a group or an obliged entity operates branches or subsidiaries in a third country whose law does not permit the implementation of group- wide policies, procedures and controls on AML/CFT. This can be the case, for example, where the third country's data protection, banking secrecy or professional secrecy law limits the group's ability to access, process or exchange information related to customers of branches or subsidiaries in the third country. In such cases, the parent undertaking in the Union or the obliged entity should communicate these legal impediments to its supervisor and may notify the supervisor of multiple impediments within a single notification.

(13) In those circumstances, and in situations where the ability of supervisors to effectively supervise the group's compliance with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 is impeded because supervisors do not have access to relevant information held at branches or subsidiaries in third countries, additional policies, procedures and controls are required to manage money laundering and terrorist financing risks effectively. These additional policies, procedures and controls may include obtaining consent from customers, which can serve to overcome certain legal obstacles to the implementation of group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls in third countries where other options are limited.

(14) The need to ensure a consistent Union level response to legal obstacles to the implementation of group-wide policies, procedures and controls justifies the imposition of specific minimum actions that obliged entities are required to take in those situations. However, the extent of such additional policies, procedures and controls should be proportionate and risk based. (15) Parent undertakings and obliged entities should inform their supervisors that the extent of the additional measures they have taken is appropriate in view of the money laundering and terrorist financing risk.

However, should the supervisor consider that the additional measures an obliged entity has taken are insufficient to manage that risk, the supervisor should be able to direct the obliged entity to take specific additional measures to ensure the obliged entity's compliance with its obligations regarding AML/CFT requirements. In order to ensure effective oversight and coordination, where a supervisor is a self-regulatory body, the public authority overseeing that body should be informed of legal impediments reported by obliged entities, the steps taken to address those impediments, any supervisory actions requested and any relevant developments arising thereafter.

(16) The additional supervisory actions described in this Regulation are specific to situations where, in the context of operations or activities carried out in a third country, including through branches or subsidiaries forming part of the group, the parent undertaking in the Union or the obliged entity do not put in place adequate systems and controls to manage the money laundering and terrorist financing risks where the law of that third country does F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 12 not permit the application of group-wide AML/CFT systems and controls that comply with Union law.

The assessment of whether such third-country legal or regulatory impediments prevent effective compliance should not depend on the internal allocation of functions within the group. Where operations or activities are carried out in a third country through a branch or subsidiary, such assessment should be made irrespective of whether specific AML/CFT functions are performed locally or at the group level. (17) Following a supervisory assessment, where the policies, procedures, systems and controls put in place do not ensure that the associated money laundering and terrorist financing risks are effectively managed, supervisors should apply the additional supervisory actions provided for in this Regulation.

Those additional supervisory actions complement other supervisory actions and measures that supervisors may apply under Union or national law, including enforcement measures available under those legal frameworks. The actions supervisors take should be proportionate and risk based, taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

(18) The provisions of this Regulation should also be without prejudice to the enhanced due diligence measures obliged entities are required to take when dealing with natural persons or legal entities established in countries identified by the Commission as having significant strategic deficiencies in their national AML/CFT regimes, weaknesses in their national AML/CFT regimes or posing a specific and serious threat to the Union’s financial system pursuant to Articles 29, 30 and 31 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

(19) For groups whose head office is located outside of the Union, where at least two subsidiaries are obliged entities established in the Union and they are not in a relationship of control with each other pursuant to Article 2(1), point (42)(b), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, one parent undertaking in the Union, responsible for the implementation of the AML/CFT framework and the prevention to the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions, should be identified.

(20) In the situation covered by Article 2(1), point (42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, before notifying the supervisor, obliged entities in the Union should assess their role, taking into account certain criteria such as the prominence of activities, the understanding of operations and the responsibility of implementing group-wide requirements. Sufficient prominence of the obliged entities should be based on elements such as the type of obliged entity, cross-border establishments of any kind, the customer base, the amount of transactions when these are performed.

In case such criteria are not enough to determine sufficient prominence of the obliged entities, other criteria should be the total annual turnover or the balance sheet or the average number of staff of the identified obliged entity in the group. Sufficient understanding of operations of the obliged entities should be based on qualitative criteria showing the types of powers and influence of the identified obliged entities in the group in the Union. In case such criteria are not enough to determine sufficient understanding of operations, an additional criterion should be the number of staff in the compliance functions referred to in Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

(21) To ensure that supervisors are aware of the identified obliged entity as parent undertaking in the Union for groups whose head office is located outside of the Union and that have two or more obliged entities in the Union which are not a subsidiary of another undertaking that is an obliged entity established in the Union, a notification and approval mechanism to supervisors should be established. (22) The identified obliged entity in the Union pursuant to Article 2(1), point (42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 should submit a notification to the supervisor. The supervisor should be able to request, where necessary, specific clarifications or additional information regarding the parent undertaking assessment performed by the identified obliged entity.

(24) In addition to groups, structures exist, such as networks or partnerships or franchises, in which obliged entities might share common ownership, management, compliance control or a combination of them, which should be subject to group-wide requirements.

To ensure a level playing field across the sectors whilst avoiding overburdening the affected sectors, this Regulation identifies situations where group-wide policies, procedures and controls, including information sharing requirements, should apply to those structures, taking into account the principle of proportionality. (25) Given the different types of structures that could exist in different sectors and jurisdictions, especially in the non-financial sector, the conditions for the qualification of structures that share common ownership, management, compliance control or a combination of them should be designed in a general and comprehensible manner to ensure harmonisation at Union level.

Furthermore, such conditions should be designed broadly to allow a wide application of the group-wide requirements. For instance, common compliance control should not be limited to compliance under the AML/CFT framework, but include other types of compliance such as any prudential, product and service compliance in place. (26) Structures other than groups under the scope of this Regulation could be identified in specific forms such as networks, partnerships or franchises comprising two or more obliged entities. Networks are common arrangements for auditors, external accountants, lawyers and other professionals. These arrangements are established for specific purposes and can have common ownership, common management, common compliance control or a combination of them.

Partnerships are also common arrangements for auditors, external accountants, lawyers and notaries. They can include obliged entities belonging to different categories and share common ownership, common management, common compliance control or a combination of them. Further, franchises are common arrangements for instance for professionals in sectors such as real estate (e.g. real estate agents) and gambling. Arrangements put in place under a common franchise may share certain elements of common management, common compliance control or a combination of them for the purposes of marketing specific types of goods and/or services. Under the conditions set out in this Regulation these structures should be subject to group-wide requirements.

(27) In addition, given the close operational and organisational links between legal entities and their branches, the application of group-wide requirements to such forms of structures is necessary to ensure a consistent and comprehensive approach to AML/CFT risk management throughout the Union. For instance, an obliged entity authorised in one Member State that operates in other Member States through one or more branches, even when it has no subsidiaries, should be subject to this Regulation. Similarly, when an entity in a third country operates only through branches as obliged entities established or located in the Union or through a combination of legal entities and independent branches as obliged entities, all these obliged entities should be subject to this Regulation.

(31) In case the identified entity is an obliged entity, such obliged entity should notify the supervisor its role to ensure clarity and effectiveness in the identification of the head of the structure in the Union.

The supervisor should be able to request, where necessary, specific clarifications or additional information regarding the head of the structure assessment performed by the obliged entity in the Union. The assessment should be based on the criteria set out in this Regulation to determine the head of the structure. (32) Obliged entities of the structure should identify one obliged entity that has sufficient powers and controls to ensure that group-wide requirements apply to the obliged entities of the structure. In duly justified circumstances and to ensure a proportionate application of the requirements set out in this Regulation, obliged entities of the structure should be able to ask for a permission to the supervisors not to identify a head of the structure.

Obliged entities should appoint a coordinating obliged entity in charge of the notification to the supervisor. Obliged entities in the structure should adopt common policies, procedures, and controls for managing the money laundering, terrorist financing, and targeted financial sanctions risks, including risks arising from the non-implementation, circumvention, or evasion of targeted financial sanctions and mutually ensure compliance with these minimum group- wide requirements.

Certain conditions should be attached to such request to ensure that obliged entities do not abuse of such permission and that supervisors can still conduct risk- based monitoring activities or take other adequate measures. SECTION 3 INFORMATION SHARING Article 4 Information sharing within a group 1.

For the purposes of the prevention of money laundering, terrorist financing and the risk of the non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions, the parent undertaking and the obliged entities within a group shall enable the sharing of the information listed in Annex I when relevant as referred to in Article 16(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. 2. The sharing of information listed in Annex I within the group shall be provided to any obliged entity that is part of the group, taking into account the availability and quality of the information. 3. The parent undertaking shall define and maintain policies and procedures for information sharing within the group.

Group-wide requirements shall not impose a requirement of the approval of the parent undertaking or any other obliged entity to share the information listed in Annex I to any obliged entity within the group. Obliged entities within the group shall set up appropriate technical and organisational means through which such sharing can take place, taking into account size, complexity and risks. 4. Information shall be up to date, readily accessible, provided in an adequate and comprehensible form, provided on a need-to-know basis and be shared in line with the requirements stipulated by the applicable data protection legislation and in line with fundamental rights, through secure channels and respecting the requirements of security, integrity and confidentiality.

Information-sharing policies, procedures and controls shall include appropriate records of information exchanges to ensure the traceability and accountability of such information and to ensure effective supervision. 5. Information sharing within the group shall not affect the individual responsibility of each obliged entity to comply with AML/CFT requirements and to prevent the risk of the non- implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions.

Each obliged entity of the group shall remain fully responsible for complying with due diligence requirements and performing its own risk assessments and making its own risk-related decisions, even when such decisions are based on information shared at the group level and taking into account any outsourcing, reliance on other obliged entities or other third-party arrangement in place. This analysis presents the Impact assessment with cost-benefit analysis (IA/CBA) of the main policy options included in the Consultation Paper (CP) on the draft RTS under Articles 16(4) and 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

This IA/CBA is qualitative in nature and the policy choices have been taken primarily in accordance with qualitative considerations, taking into account the experience and professional judgment of competent authorities from the financial and the non-financial sector, self-regulatory bodies (SRBs), and AMLA, as well as input provided by the European Banking Authority (EBA) in its response to the European Commission’s Call for Advice and feedback received during the public consultation. Moreover, quantitative figures in relation to these mandates are currently unavailable and performing a targeted collection would impose a disproportionate burden on obliged entities.
Where quantitative evidence is lacking, the analysis is supported by structured qualitative reasoning and professional judgement informed by supervisory experience and wider stakeholders’ input.

Background Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) mandates AMLA to draft RTS specifying minimum standards for group-wide policies and procedures, including: ▪ minimum standards for information-sharing within the group; ▪ the criteria for identifying the parent undertaking for groups whose head office is located outside of the Union; and ▪ the conditions under which the provisions of Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 apply to entities that are part of structures which share common ownership, management or compliance control, including networks or partnerships, as well as the criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in those cases.

On 12 March 2024, the European Commission issued a Call for Advice to the EBA on certain draft RTS under the new EU anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) framework, to inform AMLA’s work. As part of it, the EBA was requested to provide technical advice and set out options for AMLA to consider when developing the draft RTS on group-wide policies and procedures under Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. In preparing these options, EBA drew on information from its prudential work and AML/CFT guidelines or standards where applicable.
