Although the EBA’s remit is limited to financial institutions, it noted that its advice would be applicable to the non-financial sector as well.

Under Article 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, AMLA is required to develop draft RTS specifying: ▪ the minimum actions to be taken by obliged entities where the law of a third country does not permit the implementation of the measures required under Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624; ▪ the type of additional measures that the parent undertaking shall take to ensure that branches and subsidiaries in third countries, where the law of that third country does not permit compliance with Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, effectively handle the money laundering and terrorist financing (ML/TF) risks; and ▪ the additional supervisory measures required in such case.

In the context of mandate under Article 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, the draft RTS are intended to replace the framework currently set out in Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/758, supplementing Directive (EU) 2015/849. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/758 was based on joint draft RTS developed by the European Supervisory Authorities. A. Problem identification The previous EU AML/CFT framework relied largely on the national transposition by Member States of the requirements set out in Directive (EU) 2015/849 and its subsequent amendments. This approach proved to be insufficient to effectively tackle the cross-border nature of financial crime, which requires an integrated and harmonised framework at Union level.

To strengthen the effectiveness of the Union’s AML/CFT efforts, group-wide requirements for obliged entities are an essential part in ensuring adequate risk assessment, overview of activities, risks, and controls at group level. By applying such requirements, obliged entities formed in groups or structures other than groups, are required to implement a minimum level of group-wide or group-wide equivalent policies, procedures and controls to prevent and manage ML/TF risks and the risks of non- implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions. To bring AML/CFT rules to an efficient and uniform level across the Union, Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 introduces harmonised rules on group-wide requirements.

This provision also refers explicitly to Articles 9 and 10 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, which contain requirements on internal policies, procedures and controls, as well as on business-wide risk assessment. Supervisory experience, however, shows that obliged entities structured in groups often face challenges in designing, implementing and reviewing group-wide policies, procedures and controls. Additionally, a fragmented approach to the scope of minimum group-wide requirements has been identified in some cases, particularly in the non-financial sector. To ensure a more consistent and effective application of group-wide policies, procedures and controls, clearer rules at EU level are needed.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 does not address critical parts of group-wide requirements, in particular: ▪ minimum requirements on the scope of group-wide policies, procedures and controls; ▪ the type of information that could be shared within a group; F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 39 ▪ the criteria to identify a parent undertaking in the Union in the cases of two or more obliged entities in the Union not in a parent/subsidiary relationship and that belong to a head office in a third country; ▪ the conditions for the application of group-wide requirements to structures other than groups that share common ownership, management or compliance controls.

To ensure minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls and clarify certain aspects related to rules on groups and structures other than groups, Article 16(4) of Regulation 2024/1624 mandates AMLA to develop a draft RTS on the above aspects. To prevent the misuse of the Union’s financial system for the purposes of ML/TF and to ensure the highest standard of protection for personal data of Union citizens, Article 17(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires parent undertakings to ensure that their branches and subsidiaries located in third countries comply with requirements laid down in that Regulation.

However, there may be circumstances in which the law of a third country prevents compliance with those requirements, for example due to limitations on a group’s ability to access, process or exchange information, resulting from insufficient level of data protection or banking secrecy law in that third country. In such cases, the parent undertaking or obliged entity shall take additional measures to ensure that branches and subsidiaries located in the third country effectively manage the ML/TF risks, associated with the obliged entity’s operations in that country.

Where the implementation of such additional measures is insufficient to effectively manage those risks, supervisors shall, following a supervisory assessment, apply one or more additional supervisory actions to ensure adequate risk mitigation and safeguard the integrity of the Union’s financial system. While the Regulation does not specify those additional measures and supervisory actions, Article 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires AMLA to develop draft RTS specifying them. B.

Policy objectives The objective of the mandate under Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 is to contribute to the strengthening of the harmonised AML/CFT framework applicable to obliged entities formed in groups or structures other than groups as provided in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, while adhering to the risk-based approach and the principle of proportionality. To achieve this objective, the draft RTS specify minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls and establish the conditions under which group-wide requirements apply to obliged entities forming part of structures other than groups that share common ownership, management or compliance controls.

For such structures, the application of those requirements ensures a level-playing field, while taking into account the need for their proportionate application to the nature of the business, risks, complexity and size of the structure. By establishing such minimum requirements, the draft RTS aim to address deficiencies in the application of group-wide requirements that could lead to the inconsistent application, or non-application, of group-wide requirements across the Union as well as to clarify certain situations applicable structures other than groups. In addition, the draft RTS address the minimum level of information sharing within groups, to ensure compliance with the obligations to mitigate ML/TF risks and the risks of evasion or circumvention of targeted financial sanctions (TFS).

Since group-wide policies, processes and controls are expected to F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 40 address the type of information that can be shared, it is essential to identify a list of information that can be shared and provide standards on the way in which such information can be shared to the greatest extent. Given the evolving nature of ML/TF risks and the risks of non-implementation and evasion of TFS, the information-sharing framework should also remain sufficiently adaptive to ensure that relevant and emerging risk-related information can be effectively exchanged within groups.

Closely related to the mandate under Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 is the mandate under Article 17(3) of that Regulation. In this context, the draft RTS aim to ensure that ML/TF risks arising from operations of obliged entities with subsidiaries and branches in third countries are effectively identified, assessed and managed at group level, even where the legal framework of the third country prevents the full application of group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls.

The draft RTS seek to address potential regulatory and supervisory gaps that may otherwise be exploited when branches or subsidiaries operate in jurisdictions with legal impediments related to data protection, banking secrecy, or supervisory access, thereby safeguarding the integrity of the Union’s financial system. To support this objective, the draft RTS promote a consistent and convergent approach to be applied by obliged entities across the Union.

By specifying the types of minimum actions and additional measures, and establishing a common framework for supervisory actions, it seeks to minimize divergent interpretations and uneven application of risk mitigation requirements by obliged entities, while preserving the risk-based nature of the AML/CFT framework and ensuring proportionate implementation. Further, the draft RTS aim to enhance supervisory effectiveness. By defining a framework of supervisory actions that may be applied where additional measures prove insufficient, the draft RTS support supervisors in responding in a timely, proportionate and risk-based manner to situations where ML/TF risks are not effectively managed.

This includes enabling supervisors to require submission and implementation of a risk mitigation plan, enhanced monitoring, or, where risks are no longer manageable, restrictive or exit-type measures, thereby ensuring that supervisory intervention is aligned with the severity of the risks identified. The draft RTS also address the identification of the parent undertaking in the Union in situations where two or more obliged entities are not in a parent-subsidiary relationship and have their head office in a third country.

For such cases, Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 introduces a definition of parent undertaking in the Union by reference to qualitative criteria, namely the determination of sufficient prominence of activities of one obliged entity over the other(s), the sufficient understanding of activities of one obliged entity over the other(s) and if the obliged entity is given the responsibility to implement the group-wide policies, procedures and controls. The draft RTS therefore seek to substantiate these qualitative criteria by specifying how they should be assessed and applied in practice. They also provide for a notification and supervisory assessment process to support the consistent identification of the parent undertaking in the Union in those cases.

Furthermore, the draft RTS establish the conditions under which certain obliged entities organised in structures other than groups, such as networks, partnerships or franchises, and having common ownership, management or compliance controls, shall adopt, implement and apply group-wide requirements, taking into account the principle of proportionality.

The draft RTS specify alternative minimum conditions for determining whether such structures fall within scope of common ownership, management or compliance control and provide that the group-wide requirements are applied F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 41 proportionately to the nature of the business, risks, complexity and size of the structure. The draft RTS establish also a framework for the identification of the obliged entity that shall act as the head of the structure to ensure compliance with group-wide requirements applicable to the structure.

In justified circumstances a mechanism of supervisory notification and approval is put in place to ensure proportionate application of group-wide requirements to certain structures, in particular when an entity that is not an obliged entity is identified as the head of the structure or there are legal impediments in Union or national laws for such appointment. C. Baseline scenario Under the baseline scenario, obliged entities would apply group-wide requirements solely under Articles 9, 10 and 16 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, without any additional provisions specifying those group-wide requirements.

In particular, no additional provisions would clarify the type of information to be shared within a group, the identification of the parent undertaking in the Union in the case of Article 2(1)(42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, or the conditions under which group-wide requirements apply to entities forming part of structures other than groups that share common ownership, management or compliance control. The lack of regulatory provisions in this context might lead to divergent design and implementation of group-wide requirements across sectors and Member States.

It may also create uncertainty regarding the type of information to be shared within a group, the identification of the parent undertaking in the Union in the situation covered by Article 2(1)(42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, and the determination of the structures other than groups to which group-wide requirements apply and the proportionate application of those requirements. All these aspects would ultimately undermine the consistent application of group-wide requirements and create a risk of for regulatory arbitrage, as criminals might exploit jurisdictions with more permissive interpretations.

In addition, obliged entities would be required to apply minimum actions and additional measures to ensure that their branches and subsidiaries located in third countries where local law does not permit compliance with Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 effectively manage ML/TF risks, solely on the basis of Article 17 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, without any further specification of the types of additional measures and minimum actions to be taken. This might lead parent undertakings or obliged entities to take divergent approaches across different sectors and jurisdictions, thereby undermining the harmonisation objective pursued by the Union’s AML/CFT framework.

Similarly, competent authorities would assess the adequacy of the measures implemented by obliged entities and decide on the application of additional supervisory actions exclusively on the basis of Article 17 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and the provisions of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 as transposed into national law. However, no further harmonised Union-level framework would exist to define common supervisory actions. This might undermine supervisory convergence and create potential supervisory gaps that might be exploited for ML/TF purposes. D.

Options considered, cost-benefit analysis, and preferred option This section describes the main policy options considered and the decisions taken as part of the development of the draft RTS under Articles 16(4) and 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. Then, it presents the main policy options considered for each policy issue addressed by the draft RTS, followed by a qualitative analysis of the potential costs and benefits of each option, and concludes by identifying the preferred option resulting from the analysis.

Policy issue 1: level of granularity of minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires AMLA to specify minimum requirements for group- wide policies, procedures and controls. In determining the appropriate level of granularity of those requirements, AMLA considered the following options. A. Adopting detailed minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls. B. Adopting principle-based minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls. Option A Under Option A, the draft RTS would specify minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls at a highly detailed level.

The draft RTS would prescribe in a granular manner the elements to be included in group-wide policies, procedures and controls, including detailed governance arrangements, internal roles and reporting requirements. Such approach would aim to minimise interpretative differences by setting out comprehensive and prescriptive expectations applicable across all groups. This option would contribute to a high degree of harmonisation and supervisory clarity, as obliged entities and competent authorities would rely on a common and detailed set of requirements. It could strengthen consistency of group-wide frameworks, particularly in complex cross-border groups, and facilitate supervisory assessments by reducing discretion in implementation.

However, this option would entail higher compliance and implementation costs, especially for smaller or less complex groups and for obliged entities operating across different sectors with diverse organisational structures and business models. Moreover, such approach could create unnecessary complexity, reduce the proportionate application of the draft RTS, limit obliged entities' ability to adapt group-wide arrangements to their organisational structures, business models and risk profiles, and increase the risk of regulating matters already addressed in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 or potentially extending beyond the scope of the mandate under Article 16(4) of that Regulation.

Option B Under Option B, the draft RTS would specify minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls at a more principle-based level, focusing on essential elements necessary to ensure effective group-wide AML/CFT risk management. The draft RTS would set out the objectives and main components to be covered by group-wide frameworks, while leaving obliged entities sufficient flexibility to determine the level of detail and operational arrangements in light of their size, internal organisation, and risk exposure, subject to supervisory oversight.

By establishing minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls, rather than prescribing detailed operational rules, this option would ensure a consistent regulatory baseline across F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 43 different sectors while allowing obliged entities to implement those requirements in a manner proportionate to their size, organisational structure and ML/TF risk profile. This approach would define the regulatory outcome to be achieved without prescribing detailed implementation measures, thereby reducing unnecessary complexity and avoiding requirements that could potentially extend beyond the framework of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

It would also accommodate the diversity of groups and structures across sectors. The public consultation, subsequent discussions with the European Commission and feedback from supervisors confirmed the appropriateness of this approach. In response, the draft RTS were further simplified, streamlined and reorganised into broader thematic areas by removing unnecessary definitions and provisions and improving the clarity and consistency of the drafting. These revisions strengthened alignment with Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, reinforced proportionality, and reduced implementation complexity, while preserving the effectiveness of the minimum group-wide requirements.

The main drawback associated with this option is that a lower level of granularity may result in some variation of implementation practices across obliged entities. Sectoral variations may also entail additional supervisory costs, as they would require increased reliance on supervisory judgment and coordination to ensure consistent outcomes. However, such sectoral variations are considered acceptable, given the need to provide a sufficient degree of flexibility to the wide range of obliged entities subject to Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

Preferred option Based on the considerations outlined above, Option B has been chosen as the preferred option, as it provides an appropriate balance between harmonisation, proportionality and flexibility in the specification of the minimum requirements for group-wide policies, procedures and controls. By specifying those minimum requirements in a principle-based manner, rather than through detailed operational rules, Option B ensures the consistent application of the minimum requirements across all sectors, while allowing obliged entities to implement those requirements in a manner proportionate to their size, organisational structure and ML/TF risk profile.

The revisions made following the public consultation further strengthened this approach by simplifying the framework, reorganising the minimum requirements into broader thematic areas to improve clarity and facilitate their application, and reinforcing its alignment with Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. Policy issue 2: the scope of information-sharing within a group Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires AMLA to specify minimum standards for information sharing within a group.

The policy issue concerns how broadly the obligation to share information within groups and structures other than groups should apply and general standards on such sharing, in particular with regard to the type of information covered, the entities involved, and the legal and practical limits to information sharing, including data protection and confidentiality. For the specification of the scope of information that shall be shared, AMLA considered the following options: A. A restrictive approach, defining a limited and exhaustive list of information that may be shared, accompanied by strict limitations on information sharing. A broader approach, establishing a minimum non-exhaustive list of information that may be shared, complemented by specific safeguards for such sharing. Option A Under Option A, the draft RTS would define the scope of information sharing within groups and structures other than groups through a closed and exhaustive list of information that obliged entities are permitted to share within a group or structures other than groups. It would also introduce limitations on the sharing of information, such as requiring information to be shared through the parent undertaking or restricting the circumstances in which information can be shared.

The underlying logic of this approach would be to enhance legal certainty and uniformity by precisely delineating the information flows allowed for AML/CFT purposes, thereby limiting discretion at group level and reducing the risk of unlawful data processing. The main benefit of this option is legal certainty. It would reduce instances of inconsistent interpretation and litigation, particularly in sensitive areas such as data protection and confidentiality. However, this option would introduce significant limitations to information sharing within groups.

An exhaustive list would be inherently rigid and would not adequately reflect the evolving nature of ML/TF risks, limiting the ability of groups and structures to respond effectively to emerging threats, new typologies or specific group-level risk exposures. The draft RTS would need to be regularly amended to reflect emerging risks, resulting in additional implementation costs for obliged entities and reducing regulatory agility. Moreover, information that is materially relevant for AML/CFT purposes could fall outside the predefined scope, thereby weakening risk identification and mitigation.

For instance, it could expose obliged entities within the groups or structures to the risk of reopening business relationships outside the group risk appetite or failing to identify suspicious activities due to lack of relevant information. Restrictions on the circumstances or channels through which information could be shared could also delay or prevent relevant information from reaching the obliged entity that needs it for AML/CFT purposes. Option B Under Option B, the draft RTS would establish a minimum, non-exhaustive list of information that may be shared within groups, while allowing for additional information sharing where relevant for the prevention of ML/TF and the risk of non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions.

This approach would be complemented by explicit safeguards, including compliance with data protection rules, confidentiality and the application of a need-to-know principle, as well as appropriate requirements concerning the security and integrity of information sharing. The overall objective of this approach would be to facilitate the timely and effective flow of relevant information within groups, with the aim of supporting the effective mitigation of ML/TF risk and the risk of non-implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions, while avoiding disproportionate information sharing. The benefits of Option B are threefold.

First, it would support effective and timely group-wide risk identification and mitigation by ensuring that relevant information can be shared within the group if needed, without the constraints of an overly rigid framework. More specifically, obliged entities belonging to the group or structures other than groups would be allowed to share information among themselves, without limiting the sharing of information only through the parent undertaking or the head of the structure in the Union.

Second, by linking the information-sharing framework directly to F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 45 Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and providing in Annex I a minimum list of information, this option would improve legal certainty while maintaining sufficient flexibility to address evolving ML/TF risks. Third, by embedding clear safeguards based, among others, on relevance, proportionality, the need-to-know principle, data protection and confidentiality, this approach would mitigate the risk of unlawful data sharing.

In addition, by clarifying that each obliged entity remains individually responsible for complying with its obligations under Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, the draft RTS would ensure that information sharing supports, rather than replaces, entity-level AML/CFT compliance. Compared with Option A, this approach would require obliged entities to exercise greater judgment in determining what information is relevant for AML/CFT purposes and in designing information-sharing arrangements appropriate to their organisational structure and risk profile.

This may entail some initial implementation costs associated with reviewing or adapting internal policies, procedures, governance arrangements and information-sharing systems to ensure that the minimum requirements and safeguards are applied consistently across the group or structure. However, these implementation costs are expected to be offset by the legal certainty and adequacy in designing information-sharing arrangements appropriate to the organisational structure and ML/TF risk profile of groups and structures.

While this option may result in some variation in information sharing practices across groups or structures other than groups in different sectors and require greater supervisory judgment in assessing compliance with the minimum requirements, it would ensure that at least the essential scope of relevant information is shared within groups and structures across all sectors. Moreover, the draft RTS recognise a certain degree of flexibility in the way information sharing may take place to ensure that obliged entities can adapt the application of the draft RTS to their specific business models, as well as situational needs.

This flexibility is reflected in the use of general standards rather than an exhaustive determination of the information that may be shared, or the circumstances and manners in which such sharing may take place. At the same time, this flexibility would not affect the individual responsibility of each obliged entity for compliance with its AML/CFT obligations. Information received within the group may support customer due diligence, risk assessment and other AML/CFT decisions, but each obliged entity would remain responsible for complying with its own due diligence requirements and taking its own risk-based decisions.

Preferred option This analysis recognises that both options might entail financial and administrative costs for groups of obliged entities to ensure compliance with the new provisions of the draft RTS. In both cases, groups of obliged entities would need to set up policies and procedures for information sharing within the group and the structure, build appropriate safeguards, possibly modify their information-sharing infrastructure, and potentially adapt their compliance and governance functions to the new provisions. The exact costs would depend on the actual size and organisational structure of each obliged entity. Considering the costs and benefits described above, policy Option B was selected as the preferred option.

This option provides a sufficiently structured baseline to support harmonisation and ensure effective information sharing, while remaining flexible in the way in which information sharing may take place to reflect the size, complexity, and risk profile of individual groups and structures in line with the F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 46 risk-based approach.

The revisions introduced following the public consultation further strengthened this approach by linking the information-sharing framework more closely to the Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, simplifying the drafting by moving the list of information to Annex I, clarifying further the minimum operational standards for information sharing, keeping the accountability of individual obliged entities and improving operational feasibility. Overall, this approach better aligns with the objectives of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 by balancing effectiveness, proportionality, and legal certainty.

Policy issue 3: degree of prescriptiveness of additional measures and supervisory actions In line with the mandate under Article 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, the draft RTS should define a Union-level response to legal impediments in third countries, including the definition of minimum actions and additional measures to be applied by the parent undertakings or obliged entities, as well as the additional supervisory actions to be applied by the supervisors of the home Member State where those additional measures prove insufficient to effectively manage ML/TF risks of subsidiaries and branches in third countries. Under both policy options, the minimum actions are considered to provide a common baseline response to legal impediments.

The policy choice therefore concerns the degree of prescriptiveness of the additional measures to be applied where those minimum actions are insufficient, and of the supervisory actions to be applied where the additional measures prove insufficient. Against this background, two policy options are considered. A. Defining a prescriptive set of additional measures and supervisory actions. B. Defining a set of additional measures and supervisory actions to be applied proportionately and on a risk-based basis.

Option A Under Option A, the draft RTS would define a prescriptive set of additional measures to be implemented by parent undertakings or obliged entities in the presence of legal impediments in third countries that could not be addressed by the minimum actions, accompanied by a prescriptive list of supervisory actions to be applied by supervisors once the additional measures are determined to be insufficient. The main benefit of this approach would be stronger harmonisation and enhanced supervisory convergence. A prescriptive set of additional measures would ensure harmonisation of regulatory expectations across Member States and reduce the risk of regulatory arbitrage, by ensuring that obliged entities facing similar legal impediments apply the same mitigating measures.

Similarly, prescriptive supervisory actions would promote consistency in supervisory escalation and create a predictable supervisory response across the Union. This approach would also reduce interpretative uncertainty for obliged entities at the implementation stage and facilitate compliance planning and internal governance decisions when operating in third countries where legal impediments affect the implementation of group-wide AML/CFT policies. However, these benefits would come with notable costs. First, legal impediments vary significantly across third countries. Restrictions may concern sharing and processing of customer data within the group, suspicious transaction reporting information, or supervisory access to data.

Because these impediments differ in scope and severity, applying the same prescribed set of additional measures across all situations would not always be justified or proportionate. A prescriptive approach could therefore lead to inefficient allocation of compliance resources and undermine the risk-based approach underpinning the AML/CFT framework.

Third, prescriptive rules risk encouraging “checklist behaviour”, where parent undertakings or obliged entities focus on formally implementing required measures rather than selecting those that most effectively mitigate the risks associated with a specific legal impediment. Fourth, rigid prescriptions may also be impractical in situations where certain measures cannot legally be implemented in the third country concerned. This could lead to situations where obliged entities are formally required to apply measures that are themselves restricted by local law. In practice, this could encourage conservative business decisions such as de-risking or withdrawal from certain markets, even where risks could effectively be managed through alternative additional measures.

Finally, prescriptive supervisory actions could unduly constrain supervisory judgement, potentially leading to rule-based, rather than risk-based, supervisory outcomes. Option B Under Option B, where the common minimum actions are insufficient, the draft RTS would establish a common set of additional measures from which parent undertakings or obliged entities would apply one or more measures, taking into account the nature of the legal impediment and the associated ML/TF risks. Where those additional measures prove insufficient, the draft RTS would provide for a common set of supervisory actions whose application would similarly reflect the circumstances of the case and the risks identified.

This approach would therefore harmonise the range of measures available while preserving flexibility as regards the measures to be applied in individual cases. The main benefit of Option B is that harmonisation of regulatory expectations and convergence in supervisory practices would be achieved through a common set of additional measures and supervisory actions, which can be applied proportionately and in a manner that remains workable across diverse third-country legal impediments and different group operating models. Unlike Option A, harmonisation would therefore be achieved by defining a common framework and range of available measures, rather than by prescribing the same response irrespective of the circumstances.

This flexibility would avoid unnecessary compliance costs in lower-risk situations and align with the principle of proportionality embedded in the Union’s AML/CFT framework. It would also reduce the likelihood that parent undertakings or obliged entities respond to legal impediments by withdrawing entirely from certain jurisdictions where ML/TF risks could otherwise be effectively managed through alternative mitigating measures. From a supervisory perspective, this approach would preserve supervisory discretion, while ensuring a consistent escalation logic across supervisors in the home Member States.

Supervisors would apply supervisory actions within a harmonised framework, taking into account the nature and gravity of the identified risks and the impact of the relevant third-country legal or regulatory impediments. This would allow supervisory intervention to escalate until the risks are adequately addressed. The main costs of Option B would arise from the potential risk of divergent application of group-wide requirements, as parent undertakings or obliged entities may select different combinations of F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 48 additional measures in similar situations.

Obliged entities may also incur some implementation costs when assessing legal impediments, documenting the proportionality of the additional measures selected and demonstrating to supervisors of the home Member State that those measures are appropriate in light of the identified ML/TF risks. This would also result in higher supervisory effort, as supervisors would need to assess whether the measures selected are sufficient to effectively mitigate the identified ML/TF risks.

However, this supervisory effort would be partially mitigated by the design of the draft RTS itself, as the list of additional measures and the requirement to demonstrate to the supervisors of home Member States that the extent of the additional measures is appropriate would provide a structured reference point for supervisory assessment.

In addition, the supervisory actions would provide safeguards against ineffective risk mitigation by parent undertakings or obliged entities, by ensuring that supervisors can require risk mitigation plans or corrective measures and, where the risks cannot otherwise be effectively managed, apply more restrictive measures, including restrictions on business relationships or transactions and, ultimately, the closure of some or all operations or activities in the third country. Preferred option On balance, Option B is preferred because it best reconciles the objectives of harmonisation and supervisory convergence with the principles of proportionality, risk-based approach and operational feasibility across different third-country legal impediments.

It preserves the flexibility necessary for parent undertakings, obliged entities and supervisors, to address the specific characteristics of different legal impediments in a proportionate and risk-based manner. The revisions introduced following the public consultation further strengthen the rationale for the preferred option. By consolidating the framework into minimum actions, additional measures and supervisory actions, the revised draft RTS provides a clearer and more coherent escalation framework while retaining the flexibility underlying Option B. In particular, it preserves flexibility in the application of additional measures and provides for a proportionate supervisory response where those measures prove insufficient.

Policy issue 4: timing of the notification to supervisors Under the mandate in Article 17(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, one of the policy issues concerned the appropriate reporting obligation referred to in Article 17(2) of that Regulation when a parent undertaking or obliged entity identifies that the law of a third country prevents or restricts the application of group-wide AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls.

In particular, the question arose whether the draft RTS should maintain the existing approach requiring notification to the supervisor within a fixed timeframe of 28 calendar days after identifying the impediment, or whether it should introduce a more flexible or staged reporting model, recognising that the legal analysis of third-country impediments may require additional investigation. This issue was particularly relevant given that the existing framework established under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/758 already requires obliged entities to notify their competent authorities within 28 calendar days when they identify an impediment to the application of group-wide policies.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 49 Maintaining or adapting this approach therefore required careful consideration of both supervisory effectiveness and regulatory continuity and consistency with notification timelines applied in other parts of the draft RTS. The design of the notification framework also needed to take account of the potential administrative burden arising from multiple notifications concerning related legal impediments. Two policy options were considered. A. Maintaining the fixed 28-calendar-day notification requirement foreseen under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/758 as the maximum timeframe for notification. B.

Introducing a flexible or staged reporting framework. Option A Under Option A, the draft RTS would maintain the notification requirement established under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/758, which requires parent undertakings or obliged entities to notify the supervisor of the home Member State without undue delay and in any case no later than 28 calendar days after identifying a legal impediment in a third country. This approach preserves the existing reporting framework, which is already familiar to both obliged entities and supervisors. The main benefits of this option lie in its predictability and timely supervisory awareness.

Establishing a clear notification deadline would ensure that supervisors are promptly informed when legal impediments arise, enabling early supervisory engagement and effective monitoring of the mitigating measures implemented by parent undertakings or obliged entities. A uniform notification deadline would also enhance legal certainty and ensure greater consistency in reporting practices across Member States. Furthermore, by building on an existing reporting framework, this approach would reduce implementation complexity for obliged entities and avoid the introduction of new reporting requirements. However, a fixed deadline may be perceived as rigid in situations where identifying and characterising a legal impediment requires complex legal analysis.

In such cases, obliged entities may face difficulties in submitting a sufficiently substantiated notification within the 28-day timeframe. This limitation could be mitigated through the supervisory process, as supervisors may request follow-up information as part of their ongoing supervisory activities. Option B Under Option B, the draft RTS would introduce a more flexible reporting framework, for example by establishing a two-step reporting process consisting of an initial notification followed by a more detailed notification once the legal impediment has been fully analysed. The main benefit of this approach would be the potential to improve in the quality and completeness of the information provided to supervisors.

Allowing additional time for internal analysis could enable parent undertakings or obliged entities to submit more comprehensive and substantiated notifications. This could reduce the number of incomplete or preliminary submissions and limit the need for subsequent corrections or withdrawals. A staged reporting approach could also better accommodate situations where the identification and assessment of third-country legal impediments require complex legal analysis or internal escalation within the group. F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 50 However, this approach would also entail certain drawbacks.

While supervisors would receive an initial notification at an earlier stage, the substantive assessment of the legal impediment and the proposed mitigating measures would only become available once the internal analysis has been completed. As a result, the practical effect of a two-stage reporting process would be to extend the period before supervisors receive the information necessary to assess the legal impediment and the adequacy of the proposed response, without necessarily improving supervisory effectiveness. This could also lead to inconsistencies in reporting practices across sectors and Member States if the timing of notifications becomes more open to interpretation.

Furthermore, introducing a staged reporting process could create uncertainty regarding the appropriate timing of notifications and potentially lead to delayed reporting. This could weaken the clarity, predictability, and enforceability of the reporting obligation compared with the current framework, which establishes a clear and uniform notification deadline. A formal two-stage process could also increase administrative complexity by requiring multiple submissions concerning the same legal impediment. Preferred option Option A was identified as the preferred option. Maintaining the fixed 28-calendar-day notification requirement ensures continuity with the framework established under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/758 and preserves a clear and predictable reporting obligations.

It also ensures timely supervisory awareness of legal impediments, enabling early engagement by competent authorities and effective monitoring of mitigating measures. Further, it promotes supervisory convergence across Member States through a common reporting standard, while allowing supervisors to request additional information where necessary and is aligned with the timeline introduced in other parts of the draft RTS. While stakeholders raised concerns during the public consultation regarding the operational feasibility of the fixed 28-calendar-day deadline, the revised draft RTS addresses those concerns without departing from the underlying policy choice.

Rather than introducing a staged reporting framework, the revised draft retains a single notification requirement while simplifying the overall notification framework, including by allowing, where appropriate, a single notification at group or obliged-entity level for related notifications. This reduces unnecessary administrative burden without delaying supervisory awareness of legal impediments. Overall, the revisions introduced following the public consultation strengthen the implementation of Option A by simplifying the notification framework while preserving the benefits of a clear, predictable and timely reporting obligation.

Policy issue 5: specification of criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in cases of two or more obliged entities whose head office is located outside the Union Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires AMLA to specify the criteria for identifying the parent undertaking in the Union in the cases covered by Article 2(1), point (42)(b) of that Regulation. In particular, AMLA is required to specify the criteria for determining whether an obliged entity has sufficient prominence within the group, sufficient understanding of the operations of the group, and responsibility for implementing the group-wide requirements. In specifying those criteria, AMLA considered the following two options.

Adopting principle-based criteria for the identification of the parent undertaking. B. Specifying structured, sequential and objective criteria for the identification of the parent undertaking, including a supervisory framework for such identification. Option A Under Option A, the draft RTS would only provide principle-based criteria for the identification of the parent undertaking in the situation of Article 2(1)(42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

The main benefit of this option lies in its flexibility for groups whose head office is located outside the Union to self-assess their structure and designate the parent undertaking based on their internal governance arrangements. However, this option would create a risk that obliged entities in comparable situations may reach divergent conclusions regarding which entity qualifies as the parent undertaking. Moreover, the lack of structured criteria and a supervisory framework would reduce legal certainty and limit supervisory authorities’ ability to assess, challenge, or validate the designation of the parent undertaking, thereby weakening supervisory convergence and increasing the risk of regulatory arbitrage.

Option B Under Option B, the draft RTS would set out structured, sequential and objective criteria for the identification of the parent undertaking under Article 2(1)(42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, ensuring that the concepts of sufficient prominence, sufficient understanding of operations, and responsibility for implementing group-wide requirements are assessed in a coherent and sequential manner. Those criteria would be based on qualitative and quantitative factors, already available to obliged entities, using additional factors only where the primary criteria do not lead to a conclusive outcome.

In addition, this option would introduce a notification and supervisory assessment to support the structured and objective application of the criteria and the consistent identification of the parent undertaking by obliged entities. The main benefits of this option would include enhanced legal certainty, supervisory convergence and operational effectiveness by facilitating a consistent, transparent and predictable identification of the parent undertaking across Member States. The sequential application of the factors would also provide obliged entities with a clear methodology for carrying out the assessment, while retaining sufficient flexibility to account for differences in group structures and operating models. This option would entail some additional costs.

It would require obliged entities to perform a structured assessment to identify the obliged entity to act as parent undertaking in the Union in the situation of Article 2(1)(42)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and would require a notification process to the supervisors. However, these costs would be limited and proportionate, as they would rely on information already available to obliged entities and would be offset by the increased legal certainty. Furthermore, the structured criteria would reduce the likelihood of missing or divergent designations requiring subsequent supervisory intervention. In addition, the notification and supervisory assessment process would provide a key safeguard for the consistent application of the criteria.

Supervisors would ensure that they have a key role in assessing the appropriate identification of the obliged entity acting as parent undertaking. By defining structured, sequential and objective factors for identifying the parent undertaking and providing for a notification and supervisory assessment process, Option B enhances legal certainty, supervisory convergence and ensures that the identified parent undertaking is both prominent and operationally capable of implementing group-wide AML/CFT requirements.

In addition, this approach remains proportionate by combining qualitative and quantitative factors and using additional ones only where the primary assessment does not produce a conclusive outcome. Although some additional costs are expected, those would be justified by the objective pursued and by the additional legal certainty provided. The revisions introduced following the public consultation further strengthened this approach by streamlining and clarifying the application of the criteria and simplifying the notification and supervisory assessment process. In response to stakeholders´ concerns during the public consultation regarding the excessively rigid application of the criteria for identifying the parent undertaking, the revised draft RTS simplify the identification rules.

This reduces unnecessary rigidity without undermining the framework to identify the parent undertaking. Further, these changes enhance the operational application of the criteria without altering the underlying policy choice. Overall, the Option B strikes an appropriate balance between flexibility and the benefits of a structured, sequential and objective framework.

Policy issue 6: extent to which conditions for the application of the group-wide equivalent requirements to structures other than groups that share common ownership, management or compliance controls should be specified Article 16(4) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 requires AMLA to specify the conditions under which group- wide requirements apply to entities that are part of structures that share common ownership, management or compliance controls and do not fall under the definition of the group under Article 2(1)(41) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. In specifying the extent of those conditions, AMLA considered the following two options. A. Introducing high-level conditions for the application of group-wide equivalent requirements. B.

Introducing more specific alternative minimum conditions for the application of group-wide equivalent requirements. Option A Under Option A, the draft RTS would only introduce high-level conditions for the application of group- wide requirements to structures that share common ownership, management or compliance controls but do not meet the definition of a group under Article 2(1)(41) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. The conditions would focus solely on core elements, such as common ownership, management and common compliance controls without specifying further elements such as identifying the entity that designs, implements and controls such requirements or leaving other aspects to be determined by obliged entities in the structure using a risk-based approach.

As a result, this option could lead to greater variation in determining which structures are subject to group-wide equivalent requirements, how those requirements should apply in practice and to what extent obliged entities would comply with them. It would also limit implementation and compliance costs, as it would avoid the need to put in place extensive formalised governance or documentation or supervisory correspondence solely to meet regulatory specifications. However, the high-level nature of the conditions could result in divergent interpretations and supervisory practices across Member States. This may lead to legal uncertainty for obliged entities, uneven application of group-wide requirements applicable to structures, and potential gaps in AML/CFT coverage where structures are assessed inconsistently, especially in cross-sectoral situations.

Significant variations in the application of group-wide level requirements might result in uneven levels of safeguards against ML/TF risks, potentially creating incentives for regulatory arbitrage. Option B Under Option B, the draft RTS would provide a more structured, sequential and objective framework based on specific alternative minimum conditions for determining when structures sharing common ownership, management or compliance controls are subject to group-wide requirements. These conditions would provide a clear basis for determining whether the relevant degree of common ownership, management or compliance control exists, while allowing for different forms of structures.

In addition, the framework would require the identification of an entity as the head of the structure or put in place a supervisory permission to minimum group-wide requirements to be applied within structures without identifying the head. The main benefit of this option would be greater legal certainty and consistency in determining which structures fall within the scope of the group-wide requirements. Compared with the high-level approach under Option A, more specific conditions would provide obliged entities with a clearer basis for assessing their arrangements and would facilitate a more consistent supervisory assessment across Member States.

Further, it would enhance legal certainty by having a clear identification process for identifying the head of the structure and a supervisory framework to ensure that supervisors are aware of existing structures and conduct adequate supervision on them. The main cost of this option is that more detailed conditions provide less flexibility than the principle- based approach under Option A. Obliged entities would need to assess their arrangements against the specified conditions, which may entail some initial compliance and assessment costs.

In addition, structures meeting the same condition may differ significantly in their size, complexity, organisation and risk profile, meaning that the application of the same group-wide requirements in the same manner to all qualifying structures could result in disproportionate requirements. Furthermore, additional arrangements might need to be set up to identify the head of the structure or to ask the supervisors not to identify such head. This drawback would be mitigated by requiring the group-wide requirements to be applied proportionately to the nature of the business, risks, complexity and size of the structure.

In particular, conditions such as the number of obliged entities, their powers and responsibilities, the level of centralisation or decentralisation of decision-making, and the type, amounts and risk levels of the relevant services and activities would be taken into account when obliged entities in the structure implement group-wide requirements. This would combine greater certainty as to which structures fall within scope with sufficient flexibility as to how the requirements apply to them.

Furthermore, the option F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 54 to ask supervisors not to identify a head of the structure would include a proportionate mechanism to avoid overburdening the affected sectors. Preferred option While policy Option B entails higher compliance and implementation costs, these are outweighed by the benefits of enhanced legal certainty, a structured, sequential and objective framework, supervisory convergence and a more consistent and effective application of group-wide equivalent requirements across the Union.

The specification of alternative minimum conditions provides obliged entities and supervisors with a clearer and more predictable framework for determining whether structures sharing common ownership, management or compliance controls fall within the scope of the group-wide equivalent requirements, thereby reducing the risk of divergent interpretations and supervisory practices. At the same time, the specific nature of the conditions does not require that group-wide requirements are applied uniformly to all qualifying structures. Their application would remain proportionate to the nature of the business, risks, complexity and size of the structure, allowing differences between structures to be appropriately taken into account.

The revisions introduced following the public consultation further strengthened this approach by streamlining and clarifying the application of the criteria and simplifying the notification and supervisory assessment process. Following the stakeholders´ concerns during the public consultation regarding the application of a full set of group-wide requirements to structures other than groups, the revised draft RTS introduce more flexibility and proportionality considerations. These reduce unnecessary strictness, risks of application of the framework to entities other than obliged entities and overburdening structures within scope. Further, these changes enhance the operational application of the criteria without altering the underlying policy choice.

Overall, the revisions introduced following the public consultation introduce more flexibility under Option B by clarifying further the conditions for the application of group-wide requirements to structures, simplifying the identification criteria, recognising proportionality for certain types of structures while preserving the benefits of a structured, sequential and objective framework. Option B combines greater legal certainty as to which structures fall within scope with sufficient flexibility as to how the requirements apply to them. For these reasons, policy Option B is the preferred option. Further assessments The policy choices set out in this impact assessment were further assessed in light of the feedback received during the public consultation on the draft RTS.

Overall, the consultation did not identify a need to fundamentally revise the preferred policy choices, but provided additional evidence on their proportionality, legal certainty and operational feasibility. The draft RTS was therefore refined, where appropriate, to address issues identified through the consultation, including by simplifying or clarifying certain requirements and improving their practical implementation. The practical application of the draft RTS may nevertheless be monitored following its implementation to assess whether further clarification or adjustment may be needed.

In addition, the diversity of obliged entities, groups and structures covered by the draft RTS, including differences in their size, organisational complexity, business models and risk profiles, limits the extent to which implementation and compliance costs can be quantified or generalised across sectors. These limitations were partly mitigated by the feedback received through the public consultation and by reflecting proportionality and risk-based considerations in the final provisions, where appropriate. 4.2 Feedback on the public consultation On 16 April 2026 AMLA launched a public consultation on the Draft Regulatory Technical Standards under Articles 16(4) and 17(3) of Regulation 2024/1624. The consultation lasted 2 months and ended on 15 June 2026.

A total of 125 responses were received. In terms of stakeholder representation, 27% of responses were submitted by industry associations representing the financial sector and 21% originated from industry associations representing the non-financial sector, followed by 23% from obliged entities of the financial sector, 11% from obliged entities of the non-financial sector, and the remainder from SRBs and others. This section presents the summary of the key issues and views raised by the respondents and details AMLA’s assessment of the responses which includes any actions taken by AMLA. Section 1: definitions and proportionality Feedback received Stakeholders raised comments on both the definitions included in the draft RTS and the application of the principle of proportionality.

With regard to definitions, stakeholders from the financial sector, particularly the banking sector, considered the proposed definition of "control function" overly broad and requested greater clarity regarding the functions covered by the term. Stakeholders also questioned the formulation of the specific definitions for “networks”, “partnerships”, and “franchises”, noting that the criteria for determining whether entities fall within the scope of the draft RTS are already set out in Section 6 and that separate definitions could therefore be redundant or unclear.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 56 In addition, a broad range of stakeholders called for the inclusion of an overarching proportionality provision. They expressed concerns that certain requirements could impose significant compliance burdens without necessarily enhancing the effectiveness of AML/CFT controls. Stakeholders emphasised that the draft RTS should reflect a risk-based and proportionate approach, taking into account the nature, size, complexity, and risk profile of the obliged entities concerned. AMLA’s response AMLA carefully considered the feedback received and amended key aspects of the draft RTS.

Regarding definitions, AMLA removed the definition of "control function", as providing a standalone definition was not considered practical and could have created potential inconsistencies with Level 1 terminology while introducing unnecessary complexity. AMLA considers that defining specific organisational structures such as networks, partnerships, and franchises would provide limited added value, given that the applicability of the draft RTS depends on the criteria set out in Section 6. References to these types of structures have nevertheless been retained in the recitals and relevant provisions to reflect the terminology used in the AMLR and to clarify that such structures may fall within the scope of the draft RTS where the relevant criteria are met.

In addition, the definition of "structure" was revised to better reflect the underlying policy intent by incorporating the concepts of common ownership, common management, and common compliance controls. The revised definition also clarifies that the legal form of the structure is not determinative and that it shall have an element of duration. With respect to proportionality, AMLA acknowledges the importance of ensuring that the draft RTS can be applied in a manner that is proportionate and risk-based. Rather than introducing a standalone overarching provision, AMLA concluded that the principle is more effectively reflected within the specific requirements where it is relevant.

This approach allows proportionality to be applied in a targeted manner, taking into account the specific context and objectives of each provision while maintaining the effectiveness of the framework. Section 2: minimum group-wide requirements Feedback received Stakeholders raised concerns regarding both the practical implementation of the group-wide risk assessment and the potential application of the draft RTS to non-obliged entities as part of the minimum group-wide requirements. Several stakeholders, particularly from the financial sector but also from the legal and gambling sectors, noted that the proposed requirements for the group-wide risk assessment could be overly burdensome for groups or structures.

They were concerned that the draft wording could be interpreted as requiring parent undertakings to assess and consolidate the individual risk profile of every entity within the group or structure, irrespective of its relevance to the overall risk exposure. In addition, stakeholders from both the financial and non-financial sectors questioned whether the draft RTS could be interpreted as imposing requirements on non-obliged entities within a group or structure. Concerns were raised regarding the legal basis for such an approach under the Level 1 framework and the extent to which supervisory authorities could exercise powers in relation to entities that are not themselves subject to AML/CFT obligations.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E S 1 6 ( 4 ) A N D 1 7 ( 3 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 57 AMLA’s response AMLA carefully considered the feedback received and amended the draft RTS to provide greater clarity on both issues. With regard to the group-wide risk assessment, AMLA revised the relevant provision in Article 3 to clarify that the assessment should be conducted from a holistic group-wide perspective. Rather than requiring a detailed assessment of every individual entity, the risk assessment shall take into account the risks arising across the group or structure and focus on those that have a significant impact on its overall risk exposure.

Regarding non-obliged entities, AMLA reviewed the relevant provisions to ensure full alignment with the Level 1 mandate. As a result, provisions that could have been interpreted as imposing direct obligations on non-obliged entities were removed. The final draft RTS make clear that the requirements apply only to obliged entities within the group or structure, while ensuring that the objectives of effective group- wide AML/CFT arrangements are maintained.

Section 3: information sharing requirements Feedback received Stakeholders raised concerns regarding the information-sharing framework, particularly in relation to the scope of information to be shared, compliance with data protection requirements, the protection of legal professional privilege, and the treatment of information exchanges involving third countries. Many stakeholders considered there would be a tension between the principle of sharing information on a strict need-to-know basis and the drafting of Article 4, which provided that information sharing shall cover at least a broad range of information categories.

Stakeholders argued that this approach could lead to excessive or insufficiently targeted exchanges of information without a clear or proportionate link to the objective of preventing money laundering and terrorist financing. Several stakeholders also highlighted the need to ensure that the draft RTS are fully compatible with the requirements of the GDPR, noting that broad information-sharing obligations could create uncertainty regarding the lawful processing and exchange of personal data. In addition, stakeholders, particularly from the legal profession and other non-financial sectors, expressed concerns that the information-sharing requirements could conflict with legal professional privilege and professional secrecy obligations protected under Union and national law.

Finally, stakeholders sought greater clarity regarding information exchanges involving third-country entities. In particular, some questioned whether separate provisions were necessary for information sharing to and from third countries and requested further clarification regarding the interaction of these provisions with Section 4 of the draft RTS. AMLA’s response AMLA carefully considered the feedback received and substantially revised the information-sharing provisions to ensure that they are targeted, proportionate, and consistent with the legal framework. To address concerns regarding the scope of information sharing, Article 4 was amended to make clear that information should be shared only where relevant and on a need-to-know basis.

AMLA also clarified of the key information- sharing minimum standards in the draft RTS and simplified the overall drafting of Article 4. Regarding data protection, AMLA emphasises that the draft RTS have been developed in full consideration of the requirements of the GDPR.

The draft RTS specify that personal data may only be processed for the purposes of preventing money laundering, terrorist financing, and the non- implementation or evasion of targeted financial sanctions, and that such processing must be subject to appropriate safeguards, including those relating to data protection and fundamental rights. The information categories set out in Annex I were also reviewed to ensure that they are comprehensive, clearly defined, and compatible with applicable data protection requirements. AMLA recognises the importance of safeguarding legal professional privilege and professional secrecy within the limits established by the Level 1 framework.

To address stakeholders' concerns, the draft RTS expressly refer to Article 70(2) of the AMLR, which sets out the limits on information sharing applicable to certain categories of obliged entities. With regard to third-country information sharing, AMLA simplified the framework by consolidating the relevant provisions into a single article. The revised Article 5 clarifies the scope, operation, and supervisory implications of information sharing involving third-country entities.

AMLA also clarifies that the provision applies to entities located in third countries that form part of the same group or structure, even where they are not branches or subsidiaries of Union obliged entities, and that the framework in Article 5 operates without prejudice to the specific measures set out in Section 4 of the draft RTS. Section 4: minimum actions and additional measures for branches and subsidiaries in third countries Feedback received Stakeholders from both the financial and non-financial sectors emphasised that the framework should be applied in a proportionate and risk-based manner, taking into account the nature and severity of the risks, the size and complexity of the obliged entity, and existing mitigating measures.

Respondents also stressed that supervisory assessments should distinguish between compliance deficiencies and situations where compliance is prevented by genuine legal restrictions in third countries, such as data protection, banking secrecy, professional secrecy, legal privilege, or other local legal requirements. Stakeholders sought clarification on the interaction between the draft RTS and existing notification frameworks, including whether previously submitted notifications and assessments could continue to be relied upon. They also requested greater clarity on the identification and assessment of legal impediments, particularly given the complexity of legal analyses and concerns regarding the 28-day notification deadline.

Many respondents commented on the use of customer and beneficial owner consent, noting that it may not always be available or sufficient to overcome local legal restrictions. They considered consent should be only one of several possible mitigating measures. Stakeholders also highlighted duplication across the different scenarios covered in Section 4 and suggested a more streamlined framework.
