Respondents were invited to assess the impact that implementation of the draft RTS would have on additional one-off investment costs and recurring costs beyond those already required to comply with Chapter III of AMLR. The analysis included both a quantitative assessment of the expected impact on one-off investment costs and recurring costs, and a qualitative assessment of the nature of the expected implementation costs. Only the responses that included justification and explanation of the estimated additional costs were considered in the analysis. The consultation was open to obliged entities as well as industry associations representing both the financial and non-financial sectors. However, all substantiated responses relating to cost assessments were submitted only by obliged entities.

AMLA considered these responses particularly relevant, as obliged entities will directly incur and manage the one-off and recurrent costs arising from the draft RTS, and are therefore best placed to assess their expected financial and resource implications. Impact of the expected implementation costs The results have been categorised into responses provided by obliged entities in the financial sector and the non-financial sector. In the financial sector, among respondents providing a substantiated assessment, 40.7% expected one-off implementation costs to be disruptive and 37.0% expected them to be manageable, while 16.7% expected no significant additional costs.

Concerning recurring costs, 30.8 % assessed the impact as disruptive and 40.4% as manageable, whereas 21.1% expected no significant additional recurring costs. Nature of the expected implementation costs The qualitative explanations provided by the respondents indicated that the main one-off costs would arise from updating AML/CFT policies and procedures, redesigning CDD and onboarding processes, adapting IT systems and CDD databases, implementing new identity verification solutions, expanding data collection and storage capabilities, updating internal guidance, and training of personnel. Several respondents also highlighted significant implementation costs linked to the collection and verification of additional customer, ownership and control information, the remediation of existing customer files, and the integration of new monitoring, screening and reporting functionalities.

Several respondents also noted that compliance costs could increase where requirements lead to the duplication of information already available through public registers or information already verified by intermediaries. Recurring costs were expected to arise primarily from the maintenance and re-verification of expanded customer datasets, additional screening and alert handling activities, subscriptions to external verification and data services, continuous staff training, compliance oversight, and, in some cases, the recruitment of additional compliance personnel. Respondents particularly emphasised that recurring costs may be driven by the need to maintain larger volumes of customer information, and manage increased operational workloads associated with CDD.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 43 Overall, while the scale of expected costs varied significantly depending on the business model, size and current level of AML/CFT maturity of the obliged entities, the explanations suggested that the principal cost drivers relate to systems adaptation, CDD data collection and operational process changes. Assessment of the results and policy implications The assessment of the results supports the adoption of a horizontal approach, with one single draft RTS setting flexible, horizontal provisions, complemented with limited, targeted sector-specific measures only where necessary.

The consultation responses should also be interpreted in the context of the timing of the public consultation. While a significant proportion of respondents considered the expected implementation costs to be disruptive, these assessments related to the draft RTS as consulted upon. Following the public consultation, AMLA introduced targeted amendments to address the concerns raised, improving legal clarity, proportionality and the practical application of the draft RTS. Consequently, some of the implementation costs reflected in the consultation responses relate to provisions that were subsequently revised or simplified in the final draft RTS.

In addition, while respondents were asked to estimate only the incremental costs arising from the draft RTS, distinguishing those costs from the implementation costs associated with Chapter III of AMLR is inherently difficult. The reported cost estimates should therefore be interpreted with these considerations in mind. Responses provided by obliged entities indicates that additional implementation and compliance costs are expected across both the financial and non-financial sectors.

The fact that respondents in both sectors were more likely to assess the additional implementation costs as manageable or anticipate no significant additional costs than to consider them disruptive supports the conclusion that a horizontal approach can accommodate the specificities of both sectors without imposing a disproportionate burden. This finding is particularly relevant in relation to recurring compliance costs. Unlike one-off implementation costs, recurring costs represent an ongoing operational burden that persists on an ongoing basis and therefore have a greater impact on the long-term cost-effectiveness and proportionality of the framework.

In both the financial and non-financial sectors, respondents providing substantiated assessments were more likely to consider recurring costs manageable than disruptive. This suggests that, while the draft RTS may require additional resources and operational adjustments, they are not expected to impose a disproportionate ongoing burden on most obliged entities. The qualitative explanations provided by respondents further suggest that the main cost drivers relate to updates to AML/CFT policies and procedures, adaptation of IT systems, collection and verification of additional customer information, staff training, and ongoing maintenance of CDD processes.

These findings support the conclusion that, while implementation costs will arise, they are generally proportionate to the objectives pursued and are outweighed by the expected benefits in terms of harmonisation, legal certainty and the effectiveness of AML/CFT controls. Moreover, many of the implementation activities identified by respondents would arise not only from the implementation of the provisions in the draft RTS, but also from the compliance with the new requirements stemming from Chapter III of AMLR.

This provides additional support for the conclusion that the principle-based and risk-based nature of the draft RTS is sufficiently flexible to accommodate sector-specifics across both the financial and non- financial sectors.

The public consultation responses also informed the assessment of whether the policy approach set out in the draft RTS proposed by the EBA remained appropriate. The public consultation also did not indicate a need to reconsider that approach or the overall structure of the draft RTS developed by the EBA. Instead, respondents primarily identified areas where greater legal clarity, flexibility, proportionality and consistency with the AMLR could improve implementation. The targeted amendments introduced by AMLA therefore respond directly to the evidence gathered through the public consultation, while preserving continuity with the mature policy framework already developed by the EBA.

This approach strikes an appropriate balance between harmonisation, legal certainty and effective implementation, while avoiding unnecessary regulatory disruption, additional implementation costs and delays associated with reopening settled policy choices. Methodology The assessment of the policy options underpinning these draft RTS was informed by a combination of supervisory expertise, comparative legal analysis and stakeholder feedback obtained through the public consultation. The assessment drew on structured exchanges with experts from supervisors responsible for the supervision of both financial and non-financial sectors.

These discussions focused on supervisory experience with the application of CDD requirements across different sectors and business models, taking into account: • the diversity of business models and risk exposures; • observed challenges in applying horizontal, risk-based CDD obligations in practice; • supervisory expectations regarding proportionality and scalability of CDD measures; • the potential compliance and supervisory implications of sector-specific versus principle- based regulatory approaches; • provisions that have proven effective and operationally workable in practice; • areas where divergent interpretations or supervisory practices have emerged; • the impact of the draft RTS proposed by the EBA on compliance costs and supervisory convergence; and • the extent to which the

The assessment also included a comparative legal analysis of the AMLR, notably the use of horizontal AML/CFT obligations applicable across both the financial and non-financial sectors, as well as AMLA's mandate under that Regulation. This analysis aimed to ensure that the draft RTS remain consistent with the underlying legislative framework, support regulatory coherence and avoid introducing unnecessary divergences that could undermine legal certainty or effective implementation or supervision. The consultation included both qualitative and quantitative evidence submitted by respondents, including assessments of the expected additional one-off implementation costs and recurring costs associated with implementing the draft RTS, together with explanations substantiating those estimates. Particular attention was given to responses providing sufficiently detailed justifications to support the assessment of the expected costs and practical implications of the proposed requirements.

The combined supervisory, legal and stakeholder evidence informed the assessment of the operational feasibility, proportionality and expected impacts of the policy options, including their implications for compliance costs, supervisory convergence, legal certainty and the consistent application of the AML/CFT framework across both the financial and non-financial sectors. It also supported the assessment of whether the issues identified through the public consultation warranted substantive changes to the draft RTS or could be addressed through targeted amendments aimed at improving clarity, consistency and the practical application of the requirements.

Limitations The analysis is primarily based on qualitative evidence derived from structured exchanges with supervisors from the financial and non-financial sectors and comparative legal analysis, complemented by a qualitative and quantitative assessment of the feedback provided through the public consultation. While supervisory experience and comparative legal analysis provide valuable insights into the practical application of the draft RTS, they may not capture all sector-specific particularities across the highly heterogeneous financial and non-financial sectors. In addition, supervisory practices and market structures continue to evolve, particularly in relation to newly designated obliged entities.

These limitations are mitigated by the principle-based design of the draft RTS and the possibility of addressing any emerging issues through interpretative tools, where necessary. As regards the evidence collected through the public consultation, it was provided voluntarily by respondents and may therefore not be fully representative of all categories of obliged entities or of the broader market. In addition, the number of respondents providing sufficiently substantiated cost assessments was relatively limited compared with the diversity and overall population of obliged entities affected by the draft RTS.

Furthermore, the expected costs reported by respondents may vary depending on the size, business model, level of AML/CFT maturity, and existing AML/CFT compliance framework of the obliged entity. Lastly, while respondents were asked to assess the additional implementation costs attributable to the draft RTS beyond those arising from Chapter III of AMLR, distinguishing between the two regulatory instruments proved challenging. As a result, the cost estimates provided may also reflect implementation costs associated with compliance with the new requirements arising directly from Regulation itself.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 46 4.2 Feedback on the public consultation On 9 February 2026 AMLA launched a public consultation on the Draft Regulatory Technical Standards under Article 28(1) AMLR. The consultation lasted 3 months and ended on 8 May 2026. A total of 325 responses were received. In terms of stakeholder representation, 23% of responses were submitted by industry associations representing the financial sector and 14% originated from industry associations representing the non-financial sector, followed by 21% from obliged entities of the financial sector, 13% from obliged entities of the non-financial sector, 5% from SRBs, 4 % from civil societies and the remainder from others.

This section presents the summary of the key issues and views raised by the respondents, details AMLA’s assessment of the responses, and concludes with AMLA’s decision regarding potential amendments to the final draft RTS. 4.2.1 SUMMARY OF KEY ISSUES AND AMLA’S RESPONSE 1) Risk-based approach and flexibility Respondents from the financial and non-financial sector raised concerns that some requirements, notably those containing lists of information to be collected for identifying the purpose and intended nature of a business relationship or occasional transaction, verification of the beneficial owner and for enhanced due diligence, might be interpreted as too prescriptive and requiring the systematic collection and verification of information irrespective of the ML/TF risk exposure.

Respondents therefore stressed the need for greater clarity confirming that the provisions of the draft RTS should not be applied as mandatory checklists and that the extent of information gathered should remain commensurate with the risk profile. While respondents broadly welcomed the objective of achieving more consistent customer due diligence standards, a significant number emphasised the need to retain flexibility and better reflect sector-specific business models, operational practices and challenges.

Representatives of auditors, external accountants and tax advisers, notaries, lawyers and other independent legal professionals, real estate agents, gambling service providers, insurance undertakings and pension-related obliged entities highlighted practical challenges in applying certain requirements in the context of occasional transactions and the exercise of their professional activities.

These respondents also sought greater recognition that relevant information that is already available through professional mandates, contractual arrangements, products, services or existing business relationships, may be used for CDD purposes, and requested greater clarity regarding the level of detail expected when complying with the requirements set out in former Article 18 (current Article 16) of the draft RTS. Respondents from several sectors commented that the draft RTS appeared to give preference to automated screening tools, while treating manual checks as a secondary or exceptional option.

This concern was raised in relation to both former Article 19 (current Article 17), on the identification of politically exposed persons (PEPs), and former Article 30 (current Article 25) of the draft RTS, on targeted financial sanctions screening. The comments were particularly prominent among non-financial sector respondents, including gambling and casino operators, real estate agents, art market and auction- house stakeholders, notaries, lawyers, accountants and auditors.

These respondents considered that the mandatory or quasi-mandatory use of automated tools could be disproportionate for smaller F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 47 obliged entities, entities with low volumes of customers or transactions, or entities whose business model is occasional, local, or non-transactional in nature. Several respondents therefore asked that the RTS clarify that manual checks may be sufficient where justified by the size, nature, business model, complexity, customer base, or transaction volume of the obliged entity.

Some respondents also pointed to a perceived inconsistency between former Articles 19 and 30 of the draft RTS, as former Article 19 expressly referred to proportionality-based manual checks whereas former Article 30 was perceived as less clear in this regard. Several respondents also proposed simplified due diligence measures for specific products, sectors and categories of customers considered to present a low degree of ML/TF risks. Finally, respondents also commented on the enhanced due diligence provisions with one of the main concerns related to the scope of information that may be required in higher-risk situations.

AMLA’s response Avoiding excessive prescriptiveness was a key consideration for AMLA throughout the drafting of the RTS; for example, the text was revised to clarify that its provisions should not be interpreted as imposing checklist-based obligations instead, be implemented in a proportionate and risk-based manner, taking into account the specific circumstances of the obliged entity. To address these concerns, AMLA strengthened Article 1 of the draft RTS to further emphasize that the RTS should be applied in a proportionate and risk-based manner.

AMLA additionally introduced targeted amendments to Articles 10 and former 18 (current Article 16) of the draft RTS and certain enhanced due diligence provisions to specify that the scope of information and supporting documentation should remain commensurate with the ML/TF risks identified while maintaining the obliged entities' responsibility and supervisory discretion in case the information collected is not sufficient to mitigate the specific risks. While this approach reflects the discretion granted to obliged entities through the risk- based approach, it also clarifies that the information necessary should be determined on the basis of the ML/TF risks associated with the business relationship or occasional transaction, reducing unnecessary data requests and processing.

A recital already clarified that there may also be situations where the information to be collected under the AMLR and the draft RTS may already be available to the obliged entity or, for example, to other obliged entities within the group. AMLA specifies this further in the operative provisions and provides that information on the purpose and intended nature in low-risk situations may be inferred from the product or service. To alleviate practical implementation challenges and to take into account divergences in identification documents, AMLA introduced greater flexibility on the collection of given names, place of birth information and nationalities, depending on the availability of that information.

In the case of legal entities, AMLA also provided more flexibility with regard to the collection of trade names. Regarding the comments on former Articles 19 and 30 of the draft RTS, AMLA agrees that the use of screening measures should remain risk-based and technologically neutral, taking into account the size, nature, complexity and business model of the obliged entity. In particular, smaller obliged entities, entities with limited customer volumes, or entities carrying out occasional or low-volume activities should be able to rely on manual checks where those checks are sufficient to meet the relevant screening obligations. At the same time, the draft RTS must ensure that screening remains effective.

Manual checks should F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 48 therefore not be understood as a lower standard of compliance, but as one possible means of meeting the obligation, where appropriate. Obliged entities remain responsible for ensuring that the method chosen - whether automated, manual, or a combination of both - enables them to detect PEP or sanctions matches in a timely and effective manner. The amendments clarify that, under both former Article 19 and Article 30, obliged entities may use automated screening tools, manual checks, or a combination thereof.

The choice of screening approach must be effective taking into account the obliged entity’s size, business model, risks, complexity and nature of business. Manual checks are therefore no longer framed as an exceptional fallback, but as one of the available screening approaches where appropriate in light of the obliged entity’s circumstances. AMLA did not deem it appropriate to introduce automatic simplified due diligence treatment for specific sectors, products or customer categories. This would run counter to the obliged entity’s requirement to assess individual risks under Article 20(2) AMLR. Nonetheless, with the amendments to Article 1 of the draft RTS AMLA does stress the application of simplified due diligence measures in situations presenting a low degree of risk.

In response to the feedback received, AMLA amended the provisions relating to EDD to make it clear that obliged entities have discretion to determine the appropriate measures in high-risk situations. This is consistent with the discretion that Article 34(4) AMLR grants to obliged entities to determine the appropriate EDD measures and in accordance with a targeted, tailored and risk-based approach. Through these targeted adjustments, AMLA aimed to further deliver on the risk-based approach and increase flexibility while maintaining compliance with the obligations set out in the AMLR.

2) Simplification A number of stakeholders questioned whether certain requirements in the draft RTS duplicated provisions already established in the AMLR or extended beyond the scope of the mandate conferred by Article 28(1) AMLR. Respondents also emphasised that some provisions did not provide sufficient additional regulatory value compared with those provisions in AMLR and risked creating legal uncertainty or operational complexity. In this regard, respondents from the financial sector and the non-financial sector, in particular respondents from the real estate and legal sectors, questioned the treatment of senior managing officials under former Article 13 of the draft RTS.

Several respondents argued that the requirement in the draft RTS could create uncertainty regarding the distinction between beneficial owners and senior managing officials and seemed to require the collection of information beyond what is set out in the AMLR. Respondents across both the financial and non-financial sector, including notaries, also submitted feedback regarding the treatment of complex ownership and control structures and their relationship with ML/TF risk. A prevalent concern among them was that the criteria defining a complex structure in former Article 12 of the draft RTS captures an overly broad range of multi-layered ownership structures as inherently higher risk despite such structures often being established for commercial, regulatory or tax reasons.

Consequently, stakeholders called for a more risk-based approach towards complexity indicators and their relationship with the higher-risk indicators set out in Annex III of AMLR. F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 49 AMLA’s response In carefully considering and assessing the responses received, AMLA has taken into account the scope of its mandate under Article 28(1) AMLR, as well as the need to maintain coherence with the existing legislative framework and avoid unnecessary duplication of regulatory provisions.

To address concerns relating to senior managing officials, AMLA removed the former Article 13 from the draft RTS since the provision did not provide additional regulatory value and risked creating uncertainty regarding the distinction between beneficial owners and senior managing officials already established in the AMLR. Nonetheless, AMLA retained the core obligation to allow obliged entities to collect the registered office address of a senior managing official in the current Article 3(2) of the draft RTS. AMLA acknowledges the concerns raised regarding the treatment of ownership and control structures and the potential interpretation of structural complexity as an indicator of higher ML/TF risk.

Therefore, AMLA moved away from a prescriptive definition of complex structures that automatically triggered certain mandatory measures to a more proportionate, risk-based approach. Consequently, AMLA merged former Articles 11 and 12 (current Article 11) of the draft RTS to allow obliged entities to assess the risk presented by a structure, while still laying out the characteristics that may contribute to complexity. This shifts some discretion back to obliged entities, who are best placed to determine whether a structure is indeed complex and how that impacts the business relationship or occasional transaction’s risk level.

This approach acknowledges that complexity varies from one sector to another, and a large multinational structure may be standard for certain obliged entities, for instance company service providers or tax advisors, but complex for others that do not commonly encounter such structures. AMLA considers that these amendments better reflect the scope of its mandate under Article 28(1) AMLR and reduce unnecessary duplication of provisions in the AMLR, thereby ensuring greater legal clarity and contributing to simplification.

3) Interaction with the provisions set out in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and scope of the mandate Some respondents considered that the verification requirements of Article 22(6) AMLR apply only to those identification data points that are essential for identification of the relevant natural person instead of the full set of data points reflected in Article 22(1), point (a), AMLR. This would provide greater flexibility to obliged entities with respect to data points that are not consistently reflected in identity documents, passports, or equivalent documents, such as nationality and place of birth, which additional information could be warranted and assessed in specific circumstances, based on the risks identified.

Some respondents from the non-financial sector, including legal professionals, raised concerns regarding the interpretation of the concept of a person purporting to act on behalf of the customer under former Article 16 (current Article 14) of the draft RTS. Respondents commented that the extent of representation should be clarified, noting that it may overlap with the role of legal representatives, and that the definition should exclude individuals whose responsibilities are limited to back-office activities. Respondents from the financial sector highlighted significant operational challenges relating to former Article 17 (current Article 15) of the draft RTS on collective investment undertakings.

Respondents indicated that the requirement did not reflect the diversity of fund distribution models and intermediary F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 50 arrangements used across the European Union and requested greater flexibility regarding reliance on intermediaries. Respondent noted that requiring to collect information necessary to identify and verify the identity of the final investor would lead to a duplication of controls as the intermediary credit institution or financial institution already conducted these controls on the final investor.

Respondents commenting on former Article 23 of the draft RTS considered that the provision placed excessive emphasis on periodic reviews and did not sufficiently reflect a risk-based approach to ongoing monitoring as set out in Article 26 AMLR. Respondents argued that, particularly in low-risk cases, obliged entities should be able to rely on automated, event-driven and behavioural monitoring mechanisms, without being required to proactively seek updated customer information where no risk indicators or material changes have been identified. Respondents also requested greater flexibility regarding the frequency of customer information updates beyond the 5-year period set out in Article 26(2) AMLR, including longer review cycles for certain low-risk customers and products.

AMLA’s response AMLA carefully considered and assessed the responses received. The draft RTS cannot create derogations from the AMLR, such as from the identification and verification requirements in Articles 22(1) and 22(6) AMLR. In accordance with the AMLR obliged entities may, however, benefit from a reduced set of identification data points. In situations where the identity document, passport or equivalent does not contain all the information listed in Article 22(1) AMLR, Article 22(6), point (a), AMLR provides that the obliged entity needs to acquire that information ‘from reliable and independent sources, whether accessed directly or provided by the customer.’ The reliable and independent sources are further set out in Article 8 of the draft RTS.

With regard to former Article 16 (current Article 14) of the draft RTS, AMLA considers that the interpretation of the concept of a person purporting to act on behalf of the customer is not to be addressed through an RTS since such Level 2 measures cannot interpret, modify, or extend the scope of provisions included in AMLR. However, current recital 13 clarifies that the information required to verify that a person is authorised to act on another’s behalf should demonstrate that the person has the power to bind or other similar legal powers.

In response to the concerns expressed by the sector regarding former Article 17 (current Article 15) of the draft RTS on collective investment undertakings, and to prevent an interpretation that collective investment undertakings must systematically obtain information on the underlying investors (a ‘look- through’ approach) pursuant to Article 20(1), point (h), AMLR, AMLA removed the requirement on credit or financial institutions to provide the information necessary to identify and verify the identity of any final investor without undue delay. Once the framework applies, AMLA will ensure that the conditions set out in this Article are complied with through its indirect supervisory powers.

Finally, AMLA deleted former Article 23 from the draft RTS as it largely reiterated the requirements set out in Article 26(2), point (b), AMLR without adding value for obliged entities. Retaining former Article 23 could create uncertainty or give rise to misunderstandings that additional requirements apply. As the periods between updates of customer information are determined by the AMLR, they cannot be amended or extended through RTS provisions. Accordingly, AMLA did not accept proposals introducing additional flexibility that would effectively modify the updating requirements established by the AMLR.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 51 4) Customer identification and verification Stakeholders representing the financial sector and the non-financial sector, including notaries, raised concerns regarding the collection and verification of trade names, place of birth, nationality and the address. Several respondents advocated for increased flexibility where information is not consistently available through identity documents, public registers or electronic identification solutions and requested clarification regarding the application of these requirements to beneficial owners.

In addition, respondents across both the financial sector and the non-financial sector, including tax advisers, precious stones and diamonds dealers, legal professionals and gambling and casino operators called for additional clarity regarding acceptable verification methods, the concept of reliable and independent sources and the practical implementation of non-face-to-face verification measures. A recurring concern was that the draft RTS could be interpreted as establishing an “eIDAS-first” approach and insufficiently recognising alternative verification and onboarding methods. Respondents also sought greater recognition of information sources commonly used in practice, including public registers, commercial databases, and professional intermediaries.

AMLA’s response AMLA carefully assessed the stakeholder feedback submitted in relation to Articles 2 to 8 of the draft RTS and introduced targeted amendments to improve further operational clarity and legal certainty. AMLA aligned the relevant operational provisions with the corresponding recitals and clarified the applicability of these requirements to beneficial owners. For example, AMLA amended Article 4 of the draft RTS to allow the collection of city, municipality, town or village of birth, country of birth or state, as some documents indicate place of birth by the city, municipality, town, village or state, while others indicate it by the country, and clarified the approach to the collection and verification of multiple nationalities under Article 5 of the draft RTS.

Further clarification was also provided in Article 7 of the draft RTS, where AMLA identified a need to clarify when the alternative verification measures provided for in the third paragraph may be used. The revised wording makes clear that the measures in Article 22(6) AMLR are still the default option with alternative verification methods only to be used when neither of the two means required by AMLR can be used. AMLA also clarifies that obliged entities may continue using existing remote onboarding tools that meet the meet the minimum requirements regarding the quality, security and confidentiality of the verification process, as set out in Article 7 of the draft RTS. AMLA considers those requirements necessary especially in the face of emerging technological threats.

Finally, AMLA included a new accompanying recital (11) to clearly explain the rationale for these alternative measures. AMLA further removed the explicit requirement to assess every source against the criteria contained in Article 8 of the draft RTS in all circumstances, while maintaining the underlying principles-based approach relating to the use of reliable and independent sources. Finally, AMLA clarifies that in situations in which verification is done through the means specified in Article 22(6), point (b), AMLR, no additional data points need to be obtained and verified through additional information, as the reassurance provided by the means specified in said Article is deemed sufficient. AMLA also sought to clarify this through the amendments to current Article 27 of the draft RTS.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 52 5) Further guidance on sector specific measures Some respondents considered that the draft RTS did not sufficiently accommodate sector-specificities. In particular, respondents noted that certain provisions relating to simplified due diligence measures on pooled accounts may not be appropriate across all sectors and categories of obliged entities. Respondents further noted that the sector-specific measures included in the draft RTS primarily addressed parts of the financial sector, while the specific characteristics of non-financial sector were not reflected to the same extent.

AMLA’s response AMLA acknowledges the feedback regarding the need to better reflect sector-specificities in the application of customer due diligence requirements. Therefore, consideration was given to the former Article 22 of the draft RTS on simplified due diligence measures on pooled accounts, taking into account the importance of ensuring equal treatment across sectors and business models. Moreover, to address the diversity of business models, products, and services across the Union, AMLA determined that this would be better addressed through Guidelines rather than in these RTS. This approach also ensures that the RTS remain principle-based, while balancing the request for regulatory certainty and allowing further detailed and specialised measures to be tackled through guidelines.

This supports a more proportionate approach and simplification efforts while ensuring the consistent application of the framework. 6) Targeted financial sanctions Respondents commented on two principal aspects of the consultation draft. First, stakeholders questioned whether the scope of the screening obligations set out in former Articles 29 and 30 (current Article 25) of the draft RTS were fully aligned with the requirements established in AMLR. Secondly, respondents sought greater legal certainty regarding the practical operation of screening obligations, including the triggering events for re-screening and the information to be screened.

Stakeholders representing credit institutions and legal professionals questioned whether former Article 29 extended screening obligations beyond the requirements established in Article 20(1), point (d), AMLR, particularly in relation to people acting on behalf of the customer. These respondents requested closer alignment with the Level 1 provisions and sought clarification regarding the circumstances in which additional persons should be subject to screening. Respondents from both the financial and non-financial sectors requested clarification regarding the operation of former Article 30. These included credit institutions, legal professionals, notaries, statutory auditors and external accountants, and tax advisers.

In particular, respondents commented on the treatment of aliases, trade names and wallet addresses, the meaning of significant changes in customer information, and the circumstances that should trigger re-screening obligations. Respondents questioned whether certain screening events and identifiers were sufficiently clear and requested greater alignment with the requirements established in the AMLR.

AMLA’s response With regard to former Article 29 (current article 25) of the draft RTS, AMLA assessed the comments received and reviewed the provision in light of the requirements established by the AMLR and the F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 2 8 ( 1 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 53 objective of ensuring the effective implementation of targeted financial sanctions obligations. Following this assessment, AMLA concluded that former Article 29 is appropriate and consistent with the Level 1 framework. Consequently, no amendment was made to the provision. For former Article 30 (current article 25) of the draft RTS, AMLA amended a number of provisions relating to screening identifiers and screening events.

In particular, the RTS was amended to clarify that aliases, trade names and wallet identifiers are relevant for screening purposes where such information is available. AMLA also amended former Article 30(c)(ii) of the draft RTS to ensure consistency with Article 26(4) AMLR and revised the drafting concerning changes in customer information that may trigger re- screening obligations. AMLA did not accept proposals that would introduce a general risk-based approach to targeted financial sanctions screening or reduce core screening obligations established by Union law. AMLA considers that compliance with targeted financial sanctions obligations must remain effective and cannot be made dependent on the level of ML/TF risk associated with a customer.

As a further simplification measure, former Articles 29 and 30 of the draft RTS were consolidated into a single Article 25. Given the close substantive connection between the provisions, their consolidation improves the coherence and readability of the RTS, and avoids unnecessary duplication and fragmentation. This consolidation did not modify the substance or effectiveness of the relevant obligations.

7) Risk factors associated with features of electronic money instruments Respondents subject to former Article 31 (current Article 26) of the draft RTS on risk factors associated with features of electronic money instruments, mainly electronic money issuers and payment institutions, questioned the relevance and proportionality of certain risk factors included in this Article for the purpose of determining the extent of exemptions under Article 19(7) AMLR. They considered that some of these factors duplicated conditions already set out in Article 19(7) AMLR and could unnecessarily limit access to the exemptions.

AMLA’s response AMLA removed certain factors and amended others where feedback demonstrated that the criteria did not provide a sufficiently clear indication of ML/TF risk or could create unintended restrictions on the use of exemptions. In particular, AMLA removed the criterion relating to issuance charges, deleted the criterion requiring funding from accounts held with EEA-regulated institutions and amended the provisions concerning distribution channels and technological safeguards. At the same time, AMLA maintained those risk factors that it considered necessary to support a consistent supervisory assessment of risk under Article 19(7) AMLR.

8) Transitional provisions Some respondents raised concerns regarding the operation of the transitional provisions for existing customers under former Article 33 (current Articles 28 and 29) of the draft RTS and their interaction with the customer updating requirements set out in Article 26 AMLR. The main issues concerned the calculation of implementation deadlines and the treatment of existing customer relationships. Respondents also questioned whether the timelines provided for implementation were sufficient in light of the wider implementation of the AML/CFT package.

Respondents argued that this created legal uncertainty regarding the starting point for the one-year and five-year remediation periods applicable to existing customers and requested clarification that the relevant deadlines should be calculated by reference to the application of the RTS and the AMLR framework rather than the publication of the delegated regulation.

Respondents from the financial sector, notably credit institutions, and from several non-financial sectors, including real-estate agents, trust and company service providers and gambling service providers, sought clarification regarding the treatment of customers onboarded before the application of the AMLR and the RTS and the application of updating requirements to different categories of existing customers. These respondents requested greater legal certainty regarding the operation of the transitional framework and the treatment of existing customer relationships.

Some respondents further requested explicit confirmation that ongoing monitoring could be prioritized on a risk-sensitive basis, while others proposed greater flexibility regarding the sequencing of remediation activities and customer updates. Finally, respondents across both the financial and non-financial sectors requested an extension of the implementation timelines established by AMLR. These included credit institutions, financial institutions engaged in leasing activities, insurance undertakings, statutory auditors and external accountants, persons storing, trading or acting as intermediaries in the trade of cultural goods, and providers of gambling services.

Respondents argued that additional time would be required to adapt systems, amend internal procedures, train staff, and complete ongoing monitoring in preparation for the application of the new AML/CFT framework. AMLA’s response AMLA provided additional clarity regarding the operation of the transitional provisions. AMLA split former Article 33 into current Articles 28 (Transitional provisions) and 29 (Entry into force and application) of the draft RTS. AMLA further amended the drafting of current Article 28 of the draft RTS to improve legal certainty regarding the application of the transitional framework to existing customer relationships and to better align the provision with the requirements of Article 26 AMLR.

Accordingly, the current Article 28 of the draft RTS was amended to align the transitional provisions with the date of entry into force of the draft RTS and to clarify that the relevant updating periods for existing customers should be calculated by reference to that date rather than the publication date of the draft RTS. The creation of a separate Article 29 on entry into force and application further improves the structure and clarity of the draft RTS. In addition, AMLA provided further flexibility for the private sector by deferring the date of application to six months after the date of entry into force of the draft RTS, except in relation to obliged entities referred to in Article 3, points (3)(n) and (o), AMLR, to which it shall apply from 10 July 2029.
AMLA did not accept requests to extend or modify the one-year and five-year maximum periods for updating customer information, as established by Article 26 AMLR.

Factsheet on RTS on Customer Due Diligence (CDD) under Article 28(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 Important: This factsheet reflects the content of the draft RTS on Customer Due Diligence under Article 28(1) of Regulation 2024/1624 at the date of AMLA’s final draft. Please note that the RTS remain subject to review and potential amendments by the European Commission and their provisions will only become definitive upon publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. This factsheet accompanies the RTS on customer due diligence and should be considered when the RTS are endorsed by the European Commission in a delegated Regulation at its date of application. 1.

Objective The purpose of this factsheet is to present, in a concise and accessible manner, selected key aspects of the Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) developed under the mandate set out in Article 28(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR). The AMLR establishes the legal framework for customer due diligence across the Union, while the RTS specify specific elements of that framework to promote its consistent and effective implementation. This factsheet is intended as an overview of selected RTS provisions and does not cover the full range of articles contained in the RTS. This means that the RTS in all instances, takes precedence. The factsheet serves merely as a concise overview, highlighting the principal elements of that RTS.

The mandate under Article 28(1) of the AMLR requires AMLA to specify the requirements that apply to obliged entities pursuant to Article 20 of the AMLR on CDD, and the information to be collected for that purpose. The RTS must also specify: • the types of simplified due diligence (SDD) measures which obliged entities may apply in low- risk situations, and the reliable and independent sources of information that may be used to verify identification data; 2 • the risk factors associated with features of electronic money instruments that supervisors should consider when determining the extent of CDD exemptions on certain electronic money products; and • the attributes which electronic identification means must meet to comply with the AMLR.

This factsheet should be read in conjunction with the AMLR and the RTS. It is intended solely as a summary document and does not replace, amend, or supplement the requirements set out in the AMLR or the RTS. 2. Key aspects Identification and verification of the customer and the beneficial owners The AMLR requires obliged entities to identify and verify the identity of their customers, any person purporting to act on behalf of the customer, the natural persons on whose behalf or for the benefit of whom a transaction or activity is being conducted, and the beneficial owners before establishing a business relationship and when carrying out an occasional transaction. The RTS specify the information to be collected, thereby ensuring a consistent approach to data collection.

In particular, the RTS set out the information that should be collected in relation to names, addresses and place of birth: • For natural persons, obliged entities should obtain all names, including first names (given names), and surnames (family names), appearing on an identity document, passport or equivalent or through an electronic identification mean and relevant qualified trust services. The information to be collected on place of birth should include at least the country, the state, the city, municipality, town, or the village. • For legal entities, obliged entities should obtain the legal name and, where different, the trade name.

Address information should include the country and the city, municipality, town or village as mandatory data points, together with any other address elements such as the state, postal code, street name and building number, where such information exists. Where no beneficial owner can be identified and obliged entities are therefore required to identify the senior managing officials, the legal or official office address of the legal entity may be obtained instead of the senior managing official’s residential address and country of residence, in order to minimise the processing of personal data. 3 The RTS also further specify the information to be collected on nationalities.

Obliged entities should take reasonable measures to establish whether a natural person holds more than one nationality; however, where multiple nationalities are declared, verifying one nationality is sufficient. Article 22(1) AMLR, on identification, in conjunction with Article 22(6) AMLR, on verification, is clear that all the data points in Article 22(1) AMLR used for the identification purposes, need to be verified. However, in low-risk situations, obliged entities are required to collect and verify a reduced set of identification data.

For customers who are natural persons, the information to be collected and verified consists of the core identity data typically contained in a passport or national identity document, namely all customer's names and surnames, date and place of birth and nationality, or their statelessness, refugee or subsidiary protection status. In these circumstances, obliged entities are not required to obtain and verify the customer's address. This ensures that obliged entities have sufficient and verifiable information to establish the identity of their customers, while keeping the requirements proportionate to the low level of ML/TF risk.

Where an identity document, passport or equivalent does not contain all the information required for customer identification and verification, obliged entities should acquire the missing information from reliable and independent sources, as set out in the AMLR. When acquiring such missing information from reliable and independent sources, the RTS clarifies the factors that should be considered to ensure the reliability and independence of those sources. Obliged entities should also ensure that they can understand and properly assess the information obtained, irrespective of the language used.

Alternative verification measures in non-face-to-face circumstances In situations where an identity document, passport or equivalent cannot be submitted in a face-to-face context and the natural person does not have access to the electronic identification means and relevant qualified trust services as set out in the AMLR, obliged entities can verify the identity through alternative verification solutions, as long as these solutions use reliable and independent information sources and include the safeguards listed in Article 7 of the RTS.

Such a situation may occur, for example, where the customer cannot reasonably submit the identity document, passport or equivalent in person and where the customer cannot use the electronic identification means and relevant qualified trust services referred to above. To ensure financial inclusion for such persons and to ensure that financial and commercial services can continue to be provided, the RTS permit the use of alternative verification methods. 4 What information electronic identification means and relevant qualified trust services should be able to provide Annex I of the RTS set out the minimum attributes that electronic identification means and qualified trust services should be capable of providing for customer due diligence purposes.

However, this does not imply that obliged entities are required to identify or verify all attributed listed in Annex I in each and every case. Certain data points are only applicable to specific customer types for example, data points concerning legal entities are not relevant when the customer is a natural person, while certain data points may only be required when available, such as specific address elements. Nevertheless, electronic identification means and qualified trust services should be capable of capturing the minimum attributes set out in Annex I.

Reasonable measures for verification of the beneficial owner and the persons on whose behalf or for the benefit of whom a transaction or activity is being carried out The RTS also set out the sources of information that obliged entities may use when taking reasonable measures to verify the identity of beneficial owners and the persons on whose behalf or for the benefit of whom a transaction or activity is being carried out.

These sources may include public registers and other reliable national systems, such as business registers, residence registers, tax registers, passport databases and land registers, as well as information from reputable data service providers, including credit agencies, credit or financial institutions, other obliged entities within the same group, and documents of legal entities or legal arrangements where the beneficial owner is named, and where the identity of the named person is certified by persons that are authorised for document certification purposes. In situations of low risk, information from the central beneficial ownership register may be used to identify the beneficial owner.

However, as set out in the AMLR, information from the register alone is not sufficient to fulfil the verification requirements, obliged entities should verify that information using information obtained from the customer or other reliable sources. Purpose and intended nature of the business relationship or the occasional transaction Identification of the purpose and intended nature of a business relationship or occasional transaction is a central element of the customer due diligence measures. The RTS set out non-exhaustive examples of information that may be used to understand the purpose and intended nature of a business relationship or occasional transaction. This information should not be treated as a prescriptive checklist to be followed systematically.

Instead, it should be applied in a proportionate and risk-based manner, taking into account the specific characteristics of the obliged entity and the relevant ML/TF risks. To that end, obliged entities shall also consider relevant information already available to them or from other obliged entities within the same group. 5 In situations assessed as presenting a low risk of ML/TF, obliged entities may determine the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship or occasional transaction on the basis of information that can reasonably be inferred from the customer's profile, activities, products, services or transactions already available, provided that such information is sufficient for that purpose.

Screening of targeted financial sanctions and politically exposed persons (PEPs) As part of the customer due diligence measures, obliged entities must verify whether the customer and the beneficial owners are subject to targeted financial sanctions and determine whether the customer, the beneficial owner and, where relevant, the person on whose behalf or for whose benefit a transaction or activity is being carried out, is a politically exposed person (PEP), a family member or a person known to be a close associate. The screening of targeted financial sanctions and PEPs must be performed through automated screening tools or solutions, manual checks, or a combination of both.

Where applicable and available, aliases, trade names and digital wallet addresses are also relevant for targeted financial sanctions screening purposes. Transitional period for existing and ongoing business relationships For customers whose business relationship with an obliged entity was established before the date of entry into force of the RTS and is existing on that date, the customer documentation, information and data are brought into compliance with the RTS and AMLR on a risk-sensitive basis, and no later than one year for higher risk customers and five years for all other customers, as set out in the AMLR.

Frankfurt am Main – 30/09/2026 Final Report Draft Regulatory Technical Standards on criteria for identifying business relationships, occasional transactions and linked transactions as well as lower thresholds under Article 19(9) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 1 9 ( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 1 Contents 1 Executive Summary _______________________________________________________________ 2 2 Background and rationale__________________________________________________________ 3 3 Draft regulatory technical standards _______________________________________________ 7 4 Accompanying documents _______________________________________________________ 15 F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C

7 4 Accompanying documents _______________________________________________________ 15 F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 1 9 ( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 2 1 Executive Summary In order to strengthen the Union’s framework for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (‘AML/CFT’), Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (‘AMLR’) aims to harmonise the preventative measures to be put in place at Union level.

To this end, Article 19(9) of the AMLR requires AMLA to develop draft regulatory technical standards (‘RTS’) specifying: a) criteria for identifying business relationships, occasional transactions and linked transactions; b) high-risk obliged entities, sectors or transactions to which a lower threshold for customer due diligence (‘CDD’) measures should apply. The mandate in Article 19(9) AMLR aims to enable, in the first place, the proper identification of business relationships, occasional transactions and linked transactions throughout the Union to ensure that the first step in the application of the AML/CFT framework is effective and thresholds for occasional transactions are not circumvented.

Secondly, the mandate aims to ensure that higher risks of money laundering and terrorist financing (‘ML/TF’) connected with occasional transactions are addressed effectively. The draft RTS ensure a proportionate and risk-based approach and support simplification efforts. For example, AMLA did not introduce additional lower thresholds as it did not identify additional higher risks that justify such thresholds at this point in time. The approach on the criteria for business relationships, occasional transactions and linked transactions also provides a balance between flexibility and clarity, thus ensuring a sufficient level of harmonisation in the identification of these concepts and the subsequent application of CDD measures by obliged entities.

Some entities might face additional implementation costs in adapting their practices to this draft RTS. These costs are deemed proportionate to the benefits of a more harmonised approach to the identification of business relationships, occasional transactions and linked transactions. AMLA publicly consulted on a version of the draft RTS between 9 February 2026 and 8 May 2026. Feedback obtained was reflected in this draft RTS as appropriate. 1.1 Next steps The draft RTS will be submitted to the European Commission for adoption before being published in the Official Journal of the European Union.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 1 9 ( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 3 2 Background and rationale 2.1 General considerations The mandate requires AMLA to specify criteria to be taken into account by obliged entities for identifying business relationships, occasional transactions and linked transactions. Distinguishing between business relationships and occasional transactions is at the very heart of the AML/CFT framework, as it is the first step in determining the extension of the application of the AML/CFT framework.

As the distinction is relevant for the obliged entity’s assessment whether to apply customer due diligence (‘CDD’) and whether to perform ongoing monitoring of a business relationship, it is important that obliged entities distinguish properly between occasional transactions and business relationships and that these concepts are understood in the same way throughout the Union. Identifying linked transactions is relevant for ensuring that the thresholds for occasional transactions are applied effectively throughout the Union. Not identifying linked transactions properly can lead to circumvention of the AML/CFT framework by criminals operating just below the relevant threshold to avoid CDD and eventually, detection. Business relationships and linked transactions are defined in the AMLR1.

These definitions are sufficient for some obliged entities to properly identify these concepts in their business. However, in some instances, it is necessary to provide criteria to ensure that obliged entities identify business relationships and linked transactions properly and in a harmonized way throughout the Union. The objective of the draft RTS is therefore to provide criteria that aim to reduce fragmentation throughout the Union and enhance the proper identification of these concepts where necessary. As business relationships and linked transactions are already defined in the AMLR, these definitions support obliged entities in their assessment of whether a business relationship or linked transaction is established.

The draft RTS further provide certain criteria for various elements of the definitions in the AMLR. However, the mere fulfilment of any criterion in this draft RTS does not automatically indicate that the definition of a business relationship or a linked transaction in the AMLR is satisfied. The criteria in this draft RTS are not conditional or exhaustive in relation to the definitions in the AMLR. Consequently, a business relationship or linked transactions may exist even in the absence of any of the criteria specified in these draft RTS.

1 ‘Business relationship’ means a business, professional or commercial relationship connected with the professional activities of an obliged entity, which is set up between an obliged entity and a customer, including in the absence of a written contract and which is expected to have, at the time when the contact is established, or which subsequently acquires, an element of repetition or duration. ‘Linked transactions’ means two or more transactions with either identical or similar origin, destination and purpose, or other relevant characteristics, over a specific period.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 1 9 ( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 4 The mandate in Article 19(9) AMLR also aims to ensure that higher money laundering and terrorist financing (‘ML/TF’) risks connected with occasional transactions are addressed effectively. In general, obliged entities are required to perform CDD for occasional transactions with a value of at least 10 000 EUR. Lower thresholds for CDD may be introduced for specific sectors or transactions that pose higher ML/TF risks2 . Given the evolving nature of ML/TF risks, AMLA is mandated to specify additional lower thresholds for obliged entities, sectors or transactions with higher ML/TF risks.

2.2 AMLA’s approach – focus on simplification In developing these draft RTS, and when taking into account the outcome of the public consultation, AMLA sought to establish a single, horizontal framework applicable to both financial and non-financial sector obliged entities. Another guiding principle was ensuring proportionality and minimising complexity, regulatory burden and compliance costs. AMLA opted for a principles-based draft RTS rather than introducing highly prescriptive requirements. This approach minimises regulatory complexity and enables obliged entities to apply the rules in a manner that is proportionate to their business models and risk profiles, without being constrained by detailed and rigid prescriptions.

AMLA also adopted a balanced approach combining horizontal criteria with targeted sector- specific provisions. A highly granular sector-by-sector regime would have increased complexity and compliance costs without ensuring that the requirements could adequately accommodate the diversity of obliged entities' business models. Instead, the draft RTS rely primarily on criteria applicable across sectors, complemented only where supervisory evidence demonstrated a clear need for additional clarification. Particular attention was given to avoiding disproportionate data collection for the purpose of identifying linked transactions. The draft RTS highlight that obliged entities are supposed to rely on information that is already available, or should reasonably be available to them.

This approach reduces unnecessary compliance costs and operational burdens. AMLA also decided not to introduce additional lower customer due diligence thresholds beyond those already established in Regulation (EU) 2024/1624.

No conclusive evidence was identified 2 Paragraphs 2 to 5 of Article 19 introduce the following lower thresholds: 1 000 EUR for transfers of funds by credit institutions and financial institutions (except for crypto-asset service providers), 1 000 EUR for occasional transactions by crypto-asset service providers, at least identification and verification for occasional transactions under 1 000 EUR for crypto-asset service providers, 3 000 EUR for cash transactions, 2 000 EUR for providers of gambling services upon the collection of winnings, the wagering of stake or both. F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 1 9 ( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 5 to justify further reductions.

Maintaining the existing thresholds supports legal certainty and avoids unnecessary system changes, operational adjustments and administrative costs during the implementation of the new AML/CFT framework. 2.3 Business relationships and occasional transactions Business relationships and occasional transactions are mutually exclusive. To clarify this, occasional transactions are defined negatively in Article 1 of this draft RTS. Additionally, this article clarifies that the provision of services connected to a transaction can also be identified as an occasional transaction. This is relevant for those entities that do not perform transactions themselves, but instead provide services connected to a transaction, such as real estate agents.

This provision of services can exist in the context of a business relationship, as well as in the context of an occasional transaction. Article 2 of this draft RTS provides criteria that should be taken into account by obliged entities when assessing whether the definition of a business relationship from the AMLR applies. The criterion in the first paragraph applies to all obliged entities. The other criteria specifically address certain obliged entities. 2.4 Linked transactions The AMLR stipulates that transactions should be linked if two or more transactions have an ‘identical or similar origin, destination and purpose’. Transactions could also be linked on the basis of ‘other relevant characteristics’. Both categories of linked transactions should take place over a ‘specific period’.

Article 3 of this draft RTS provides criteria which should be taken into account when considering the different elements of the definition of linked transactions. The assessment of whether transactions are linked should be based on an overall evaluation of all relevant facts and circumstances. The criteria set out in Article 3 should therefore be considered collectively and in the context of the specific case. No single criterion should be regarded as decisive in isolation, nor should any criterion be disregarded solely because, on its own, it is not determinative. Some of the criteria in Article 3 should only be taken into account based on information available to the obliged entity.

This means that obliged entities should only take those criteria into account if the information is already available to them. Where an obliged entity has, or should have, access to information relevant to the listed criteria, it should take that information into account. If it does F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 1 9 ( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 6 not have access and is not required to, it does not need to obtain the information solely for the purposes of identifying linked transactions. 2.5 Additional lower thresholds No additional lower thresholds for CDD regarding occasional transactions are identified in these draft RTS, at this point in time.

The AMLR already provides lower thresholds for specific sectors and transactions that pose higher ML/TF risks. AMLA has considered the necessity of introducing additional lower thresholds. As this would pose a burden on the relevant obliged entities and their customers, such a burden should be justified by providing evidence of the need and proportionality of these thresholds. Since the entry into force of the AMLR, no conclusive information has emerged indicating that any additional lower thresholds are necessary and proportionate to mitigate ML/TF risks across the Union.

If in the future it becomes apparent that mitigation of ML/TF risks via the introduction of an additional lower threshold is necessary and proportionate for certain obliged entities, sectors or transactions, a proposal for amendment of the RTS will be made. Distinguishing between business relationships and occasional transactions is central to the AML/CFT framework. (2) All obliged entities are required to have internal policies and procedures in place to ensure compliance with the obligations regarding customer due diligence in Chapter III of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. These internal policies and procedures should be proportionate to the nature of the business – including its risks and complexity – and the size of the obliged entity. In the context of this Regulation, this includes internal policies and procedures to ensure that obliged entities can properly identify business relationships, occasional transactions and linked transactions for the purpose of the application of customer due diligence measures.

Such internal policies and procedures could include the identification and verification of the customer, regardless of the value of the transaction. (3) Identifying linked transactions is, among other purposes, relevant for ensuring that the thresholds for occasional transactions are applied effectively to avoid the circumvention of customer due diligence requirements and for identifying the obliged entities in Article 3(3), points (i) and (j), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. 3 OJ L, 2024/1624, 19.6.2024.

F I N A L R E P O R T – D R A F T R T S U N D E R A R T I C L E 1 9 ( 9 ) O F R E G U L A T I O N ( E U ) 2 0 2 4 / 1 6 2 4 9 (4) Business relationships and linked transactions are defined in Article 2(1), points (19) and (20), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, and these definitions should be leading in the obliged entity’s assessment of whether a business relationship or linked transaction exists. To support their consistent identification across the Union, this Regulation provides criteria for certain elements of these definitions. These criteria are neither exhaustive nor determinative; their fulfilment does not in itself establish, nor their absence preclude, the existence of a business relationship or linked transaction.

(5) Since business relationships and occasional transactions are mutually exclusive, occasional transactions are defined negatively in this Regulation. This Regulation only applies to activities that fall within the scope of the AML/CFT framework. Accordingly, activities outside that framework cannot constitute either a business relationship or an occasional transaction. (6) The AML/CFT framework applies to obliged entities that carry out transactions and to those, such as real estate agents and notaries, that provide services connected to transactions. Such services may be provided in the context of a business relationship or an occasional transaction.

For the purposes of customer due diligence thresholds, obliged entities that provide services connected to transactions should consider the value of the relevant transaction, excluding any transaction or service fees. (7) An element of the definition of a business relationship is the expectation or subsequent acquisition of an element of duration. In assessing that element, obliged entities should consider whether the customer has been granted ongoing access to services within the scope of the AML/CFT framework, including through a customer account. Registration granting such access may indicate an expected degree of duration, whereas subscriptions to purely informational communications, such as newsletters, should not.

(8) In certain non-financial sectors, obliged entities typically provide services connected to transactions rather than carrying out transactions themselves. To support the consistent identification of business relationships in those sectors, this Regulation specifies criteria that may assist in assessing the elements of duration and repetition referred to in the definition of a business relationship. Relevant considerations may include whether the provision of a service requires a series of actions over time, whether services are provided to the same customer at different intervals, including in relation to different objects, and whether different categories of services are provided.

This can take different forms, including, for instance, the issuance of a loyalty card or the offering of discounts for the performance of multiple transactions or multiple purchases.
